paragraphs.text: Again: other headings on the soul, and on the distinction between the passions of human beings: those of the body, those of the soul, and those of the spirit.

As for us, Eutropius and Eusebius: after we had received his first letter, we were eager to come to him. When we entered his cell and greeted one another with prayer, many things were said in our conversation together that have not been written down. Our first question was this: why, of all bodies, was the nature of the soul placed in the human body? John said: My beloved, I will tell you how it seems to me. Because God wished that man alone should search into the knowledge of his wisdom, he made this whole creation wide and spacious in its height and its depth, its elements opposed to one another in their nature. Within its deep plain and the circuit of its sphere he set measures for its regions: in the division of the seas, in the course of the rivers, in the flowing of the springs, in the stature of the trees, in forms of every color. And in the vault of the firmament the lights blaze in high places and low, in the changing seasons of the sun and moon. And since everything that has motion in its course and color in its appearance consists in two mysteries, in its visible appearance and in the craftsmanship of God's working within it, for this reason the thing that God was about to create, which these created things would serve and through which they would bring him to the understanding of God's wisdom,

had to be made of two movements belonging to two essences; so it was fitting that its existence in the world should be. Thus, by openly seeing these wondrous beauties that shine out from all created things, the visible essence of the body might take delight; and by the wisdom hidden in them, the hidden essence of the soul might take delight. For if he gave the created things a nature and a form in the color of their created appearance, and a hidden mystery concealed within them that points to the wisdom of God, how much more would he establish man, the king of all the beings of this creation, with a surpassing beauty in the form of his bodily members, and with a glorious nature by which he is moved to understand the works of God! Eusebius said: Would the body not have been enough, through the motion of its senses, to understand the works in their ordering? John said: The nature of the body cannot see what is invisible, unless the mind sees it through the sight of the eyes. For look: these eyes cannot see beyond the firmament. When we wish to look beyond the firmament, we do not look with the eyes of the body; we contemplate with the mind within. It is not the sight of the eyes that enters into a house, but the sight of the heart. And when the moon rises at its full in the east, it seems to the eyes to be not five miles away, but the mind understands that it is in the east for everyone alike. Since the outward senses of hearing, sight, smell and touch were not sufficient to grasp the inner depth of the mystery of created things, God therefore clothed in the hiddenness of the inner members a nature subtler in its senses than all bodies, so that by the keenness and subtlety of its movements it might grasp the hidden wisdom of the works of the Lord of all. Eusebius said: Could souls not have understood the wisdom of God while existing separately, without a body? Just as

the angels, though they are not in a body, are mighty in understanding God and have had no need of a body to serve them as a means, so too these souls could have contemplated the wisdom of God without being placed in a body. John said: My brothers, if these souls had been created on this principle, to exist in the world without a body, their knowledge would have been capable of perceiving the hidden wisdom of these created things. But they would not have been moved to search them out, because their nature is higher than these things and they have no need of them. And because they do not need them, they would not even have cared about the wisdom in them, just as the seraphim do not care to seek out the wisdom of this world, because their nature is higher than it. As for bringing forward the nature of the angels as an example, that is another mystery concerning them, for they remain in the order in which they were created by God. But the nature of souls was not established by God in this way. If man were only a body without a soul, God would not have made a man in the world at all, but only a body like the rest of the bodies that are deprived of the understanding of his wisdom, like the kinds of beasts and the birds of the sky. Everything that distinguishes man from all creatures is due to the honor he has from the soul within him. And because it is in him, it is moved in him, through his hardships and his need of everything, to grow wise about all things. The body shares with the soul in the faculties that come from it, and the soul shares with the body through the wisdom hidden in it, by virtue of its having come from God. If man were without a soul, he would be like everything else, as I said above. And if souls had been created in the world without a body, it would have been pointless for them to be stirred by reflections on the ordering of created things, while needing none of them.

But now that they have been clothed with a body, the body has become a reason for them to think about the things that belong to the body; and through it they care about the wisdom within it, each person in his own measure. Eusebius said: I would like to hear how souls are raised above any need of visible things. John said: Look and consider the use of all the things by which every need of the body is filled, while the soul itself has no need of them. For it is not visible, that it should need visible things: neither the rising of the sun, nor the phases of the moon, nor the whole intermediate expanse above us; that is, neither the circling of the clouds, nor the fire of the lightning, nor the sound of the thunder, nor the downpours of rain, nor the flow of the springs, nor the light of day, nor the stillness of night, nor the seasons of the mountains [?], nor the counting of the hours, nor the changing of the months, nor the cycle of the whole year and all that happens in it. The nature of the soul is free of all these things, so that by its subtle movements people might seek the wonder of God's works. But instead of being occupied with this inquiry, so that through steady attention they might be kept from the desires of the body, they have become wrongdoers against God through unseemly deeds, meditating neither on the wisdom of nature nor on the wisdom of the scriptures. O how greatly God has labored to make people wise, and O how far they have strayed from the discipline of his teaching! They care only for empty pleasures. Whoever takes delight only in the outward sight of created things, and does not trouble to trace the wisdom of God in them, stands on the level of the animals, which, like him, also see with their outward senses the sun, the moon, the stars, the light, and all the colors of the earth. But whoever cares about

the hidden wisdom within them is a soulish man, who looks with the senses of his soul upon the ordinances of the Lord of all. Eusebius said: On this subject, the reason for the soul's dwelling in the body, we have heard enough. But since we wish to hear many things that will also profit our souls, we ask you to explain to us the conduct of the inner and the outer man. John said: I will begin first with the divine commandment that brings us near to his love: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul" (Deut. 6:5). Eusebius said: Why did God place this commandment before the rest of the commandments, since it is weightier than those that follow it? For there are people who do not kill, commit adultery or steal, yet do not attain to the love of God. John said: My beloved, God set it first because it is what makes people keep the rest as well. For if they do not persevere in that first one, knowing that he is the one God, neither can they love him. And if they do not abide in his love, neither will they refrain from murder and adultery. But if they draw near to knowing his lordship and loving him with all their heart, it is clear that they will also obey the rest of the commandments. Through their obedience to God and their abstaining from the deeds he commanded them not to do, people will live in peace with one another. The commandment of the blessed gospel, however, did not only rebuke evil deeds; it also abolishes the thoughts that give rise to actions. "Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute you" (Matt. 5:44; Luke 6:27). These commandments bring the inner man near to purity

of mind. But the legal commandment given to the people dealt with deeds, that they should not appear in the body, compelling a person even against his inner thoughts, though his will is not in the deed. As in that saying: "If your enemy's donkey falls under its load on the road and you do not want to lift it with him, you must surely lift it with him." Here the law produces the good deed even though the mind within is not pure. But our Lord in his gospel purifies the mind itself. "Love your enemies": not only, he says, do I command you to do good to them with your outward members, but also to bear love for them in your inner senses, as God loves even those who hate him. And these deeds bear witness to his love: "For he makes his sun rise on the good and on the evil, and sends his rain on the righteous and on the unrighteous" (Matt. 5:45). Eusebius said: What is the beginning of the conduct of the inner man? John said: Emptying oneself of the love of money. After emptying himself of the love of money, he must necessarily empty himself of the passion of the love of glory. And then after that he must be excellent in mind: in humility and patience, in calmness and understanding, in the joy of his hope, in wakefulness of good reflections, in perfect love of God and of people. By these he will draw near to purity of soul, which is the completion of all the conduct by which God commanded man to live in this life. For all his commandments bring a person up to purity of soul. But when he has fought the contest and overcome all the evil passions and stands in purity of mind, he passes beyond all the conduct commanded by God for this life, and from then on begins to enter, out of purity of soul, into the conduct of the new man, who is no longer a servant on whom

a law is imposed, but a beloved son, free of everything in this world. He begins to become a son of God's mystery, since in his knowledge he comes to have communion with God. And God converses with him through revelations of mysteries, as he grows in the things of the Spirit. This is the order of the conduct of the inner man, whom Paul calls the spiritual man, "who judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one" (1 Cor. 2:15); for no one knows him, and his glorious conduct is not visible to people, yet he judges all things. Eusebius said: How does he judge all things? John said: Listen, according to the subject you have put to me. Because he is raised above everything visible, he understands all things, judges and condemns what is not good, and little by little rises to be perfected in the spiritual order. So he is judged neither by God nor by people. Rather, all those beneath him are judged by him, just as the world is judged by the saints: though they were like the saints in nature, they did not equal them in deeds. And so that I may not seem to be saying these things without grounds, let us turn to the teaching of our Lord, which makes known to us that after a person keeps the commandments and draws near to purity of soul, he becomes an intimate of God in his mysteries. For he said: "Whoever has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me; and whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and show myself to him" (John 14:21). That is: after a person fulfills the commandments laid upon him, and the eagerness to fulfill them comes from love, then I too will show myself to him by making known the mysteries of myself. But for anyone to draw near to the mind that is above purity of soul is one of the gifts given to us in the other world. Yet whoever

is diligent in this conduct I have described, God begins even here to give him some of the gifts to come, as much as he can receive in this life. So, from emptying himself of the passion of the love of money, as I said, he begins the conduct of the inner man and is carried up to purity of soul. And from purity of soul onward, he begins the conduct of the new life, through growth in constant knowledge. That I speak of him as the inner and the outer man, the apostle too calls him so: "that Christ may dwell in your inner man" (Eph. 3:16); and "Though our outer man is wasting away, yet the inner is renewed day by day" (2 Cor. 4:16); and "I delight in the law of God in the inner man" (Rom. 7:22). Now this is the good conduct of the outer man: that he should not engage in dissipation and drunkenness, nor in curses and quarrels, nor in the desires of his flesh, while he praises God with the voice of his mouth, together with other things like these. If a person has only these, he stands at the measure of the conduct of the visible man, serving the Lord of all in the order of servitude, in the manner of a hired man who works for his wage. This order of conduct the apostle calls the soulish man, who "does not receive the things of the Spirit, for they are folly to him; and he cannot know them, because they are judged by the Spirit" (1 Cor. 2:14). Eusebius said: How is it that he cannot perceive that they are judged by the Spirit? John said: I am speaking according to the subject I am discussing. Everyone who is wholly given to the conduct that seems good to people, and engages in almsgiving, fasting and vigils that banish sleep, has his whole mind bound up in his conduct, and the joy of his hope springs up in him through his labor. And all the glory that will

come to him from the abundance of God's goodness in the world to come, he imagines he receives because of his deeds, and not from the treasury of God's mercy. Therefore, if someone speaks to him about spiritual things he does not perceive, the speaker is counted a fool in his eyes. For everything people hold to in this life, which seems to them to be the excellences of God's will, is empty in comparison with what they will be in. For look, all things here pass away, and God establishes people in another order after their resurrection. In the life to come they do not serve him with the burning of incense, nor with offerings and visible deeds. And the soulish man does not know how to listen to anything beyond these visible things. For whoever is soulish in his good deeds, if these are rendered void for him by the showing of something greater than them, is left as if with his hope cut off. He has not drawn near to the greater, and he has let go of what he held. So in these matters he becomes hopeless in mind, because he has not perceived that there is anything else beyond what he supposed. And therefore he does not know that these things are judged by the Spirit. And if he is told that everything he supposes glorious is nothing compared with the things of the Spirit, he cannot receive the judgment of this knowledge. When God makes a revelation to the soulish man, he makes known to him beforehand events that are to happen in the world. And when a gift is given to him, he receives the working of signs, because these are glorified among people, and through them they can receive faith in the invisible God. And since he serves God with his outward members, God too places the gift in his members: that his tongue should tell what is to come and his hand perform a sign. Yet this gift is not only not wondrous, it is not even desired by the person

who has perceived spiritual revelations. For think of the many ranks seen arrayed in their order before a king, each rank outshining its neighbor in its garments. The spectators stand and gaze: they see the first rank and praise the style of its garments; the second appears and they marvel still more; the third rank comes out and they are amazed at its garments, and from then on the first rank becomes shabby in their eyes, not because they were dressed in shabby garments, but because the glory of the others makes them look shabby. By this example understand the mystery I am speaking of. However great it is for someone to have revealed to him something that will happen in the world, the revelation of the new life is far greater, more glorious than the other by as much as the world to come surpasses this one in which we live. But whoever has not perceived that mystery places all his greatness in the things before his eyes. For the gift the soulish man receives heals the pains of the body by its signs, through the faith of the onlookers. And he is given revelations of famines and wars, which people also foretell from their experience of such things, like a helmsman about the winds of the sea, or a physician about the pains of the body. The apostles, however, received both the powers of signs and the wisdom of the other life, because they were chosen to teach the nations: through signs the mystery of Christ, that he is from God, would be believed in them, and through the wisdom of the future life they would make people wise about their hope. Yet in their eyes it was far greater that they were wise in their hope than that they performed mighty works. For many have worked wondrous signs, cast out demons, cleansed lepers and healed the sick, and yet did not perceive the wisdom of that world, because it is greater than everything wondrous in this world. For look at the Corinthians: while

they were working many wonders, speaking in tongues and interpreting tongues, and uttering prophecies in which they foretold what was to happen in the world, together with other wonders, they could not even hear the mystery of the wisdom concerning that world. For the apostle rebukes them and says that not only, when he came to them, could he not speak to them the wisdom of that world, which he calls "solid food," but "even now you are not able to receive it" (1 Cor. 3:2). "Yet we do speak wisdom among the perfect, a wisdom not of this world" (1 Cor. 2:6). So although they were showing many signs, they had not reached this measure. For a person to work signs before unbelievers, being envious or proud does not hinder him. But for a person to perceive that wisdom of his hope there is no way, unless he is pure in mind. For the power of all signs is teaching about God; it does not follow that the one who works them, or the one who sees them, thereby knows anything of what is to be understood about the life after the resurrection. This wisdom is far more inward in its power than the gift of signs, as the soul is more inward than the body. If the working of signs were greater than wisdom about the future life, why, after the resurrection, did he not give the righteous the working of mighty deeds instead of the wisdom of his mysteries? But it is clear, as I said, that the power of signs is directed only against error. Once people have come out of error, they begin to learn the wisdom of his mysteries. For this reason the power of signs is, for people, like the soulish order. Just as the soul is placed between bodiliness and spirituality, being in this life neither like the body nor like the perfect spirituality of the angels, so the power of signs stands between error and truth, drawing away from error

and bringing near to truth. Therefore the life of that world, since it is higher than error, is higher also than signs, for there is no need there to come out of error. Again, the soulish man has a struggle with demons. Eutropius said: For what reason? John said: Because his conduct is visible, Satan envies him his deeds. He begins to ask God, by petition, for leave to do battle with him, and if God permits him, he becomes his adversary in every way. Eusebius said: And why does he not wage war in the same way against a spiritual man, since the conduct of the spiritual man surpasses that of the soulish? If what excels in deeds is what makes Satan envious, he ought to envy the man of the Spirit more than the man of the soul. John said: My brothers, the conduct of the spiritual man is not seen bodily among people. And the good things that are seen in him are not of the Spirit but of the soul, as in someone who is not bodily in his deeds. But because that hidden conduct of his is hidden from Satan, and no one sees it but God, envy is not stirred against him either. And if Satan does envy him, it is because of the things that are visible in him. For look at our Lord: although there was no measure to that greatness, that knowledge and that glorious conduct, Satan approached him with a tempter's gaze only at the time of the labor of fasting. Because he did not see his spiritual conduct and his glorious knowledge with God the Father, he was not fully envious in his wickedness either; for Christ conducted himself in his visible life like the rest of people. But so that Satan might have an opening for

tempting our Lord, he roused the wickedness of his envy through the labor visible in the body. As for his approach to our Lord, the names "accuser" and "tempter," and why our Lord was led into the desert to be tempted, that is another subject. Now hear also about the order of the bodily man. If a person does not even conduct himself in this visible good conduct, not only is he not a servant of God, he is a stranger to his whole household. Such a person the apostle calls bodily: "As long as there is envy, jealousy, strife and division among you, are you not bodily, and walking in the flesh?" (1 Cor. 3:3). For by Christ's own designation these are slaves of sin. So Scripture names three orders of people: bodily, soulish and spiritual. Those whose whole mind wanders among evil thoughts, if they love to carry them out, stand in the conduct of demons. Those whose whole mind is occupied with human evils, even if they do not love to fulfill their impulses, are bodily, because they are still moved by these thoughts. For so the apostle said: "As long as there is envy and strife among you, you are bodily." But if a person struggles against the wickedness of his thoughts, does not surrender his mind to their impulses, and forcibly restrains himself from doing their will, then if he perseveres in this mind he is close to the soulish level. Eusebius said: And when does he become soulish? John said: When he neither commits evil nor thinks hateful thoughts. Eusebius said: And why is the one who is not enslaved to his passions called by this name? John said: Because the nature of the soul is higher than evil deeds

and shameful thoughts, and it is moved to share in them because of the body, as I showed in your letter. Therefore whoever has risen above these bodily things and has come near to the order of the nature of the soul is called soulish, just as whoever indulges in the desires of the nature of the body is called bodily. Now hear another subject as well. Whoever is a man of the flesh is not moved by the fear of judgment, nor does he care about the wisdom of learning. When he asks something of God in prayer, he has no way to gather his mind; the habits and thoughts he is used to wander through his mind, and he looks upon God as upon the image of a man. But whoever is soulish in mind has a love of learning. He is able to gather his mind in prayer, but only with a great struggle, and his recollection lasts a short time; purely, not even for the twinkling of an hour. Why? Listen. Because his soul is in wandering movements, or in the meditation of studies, or in the labor of the body, these things spring up in him even at the time of his prayer. He cannot look upon God with a gathered mind, because his intellect wanders among various images let loose upon one another; above all because he has not reached the measure that is above the soulish, the measure that looks upon God in something higher than human thought. But the spiritual man, since he is higher than bodily thoughts, has no moment when his whole mind is not welling up in the wisdom that is in God. If anyone has not perceived what I have said, let him accept this which he has not understood on the strength of the earlier things he did perceive. Eutropius said: Since in the course of your discourse we have found many things that had not even occurred to our minds, it has proved well worth the trouble for me and for this brother of mine, Eusebius, to come to you. For although we had not left our cell

for many years, our coming to you has profited us far more than our staying would have. The rules we had set for ourselves we now count as nothing compared with the knowledge you set down for us in our letter. What happened to Paul has happened to us as well. Just as he formerly boasted and rejoiced in the conduct of the law, as one who thought it was perfection and that there was nothing beyond it, until he received the knowledge of Christ, so we too thought that what we held was perfection, until we learned through the subject of your discourse how far we fall short of perfection. And just as the apostle, through the surpassing knowledge of Christ, counted as loss the things that he had formerly counted as righteousness, so we too have despised the joy of our labor, so that we may boast only in the hope of God. John said: I too, my brothers, perceiving that your good mind seeks the truth and does not boast in the rules of regulations, have loved to speak with you of the things by which you will come to a place of peace, your souls sheltered within a wall that no storm can shake. Eusebius said: We too likewise ask you to tell us the explanation of these orders. And do not wait for us to be the questioners, for we did not even know that they existed, nor did we know what to ask about them. But tell us, of your own accord, whatever comes to your mind about the passions of the soul and their causes. John said: I will begin by speaking about compunction of soul, and in which of these three orders it is found. It is found neither among the bodily nor among the spiritual: not among the bodily because of their evil mind, and not among the spiritual because they have been raised above this passion through joy. Compunction of soul is found only

among the soulish. I will also tell you its cause. Because the soulish man is moved by the fear of God, he begins to be troubled about his deeds, and from the sorrow over his sins compunction of soul is born in him. Let us now go on to explain weeping with tears as well: what thoughts move it in the mind in these three orders. The weeping of the bodily man, even when he weeps in prayer before God, is moved by these thoughts: brooding over his poverty, remembrance of his losses, concern for his children, the pain of the wrongs done to him, anxiety about his household, remembrance of his dead, and the rest of such things. From the combination of these thoughts sorrow grows in him, and from sorrow tears are born. The weeping of the soulish man in prayer is moved by these thoughts: fear of judgment, brooding over his sins, remembrance of God's goodness toward him, reflection on death, the promise of the things to come, dread of being deprived of them, and the rest of such things. From the combination of these thoughts his mind is moved to the passion of tears. But if other people are with him, then unless he has great watchfulness, his weeping does not come from these reflections; rather, he begins to slide into the passion for glory from people. As he looks at their gathering and his own standing in their midst, the sight of people moves him to the passion of weeping out of vainglory. The weeping of the spiritual man, however, is drawn forth by these thoughts: amazement at the greatness of God, wonder at the depth of his wisdom, the glory of the world to come, the error of humankind, and the rest of such things. From the combination of these he pours out tears before God. His weeping does not come from the passion of sorrow but from great joy, for weeping is also born of joy. Just as many people, when

see their loved ones after a long time, and shed tears for the joy of seeing them. The weeping of a man of the spirit that does come from sorrow has this cause: he remembers how far people go astray. So our Lord wept when he entered Jerusalem. So too it is said that he was grieved at the deadness of their hearts (Mark 3:5). So Paul said, “But now I speak of them with tears” (Philippians 3:18). And so again it is written of him in Acts that for three years he did not cease weeping (Acts 20:31). But this weeping did not arise in the mind of the spirit. It arose in thoughts of the soul: over people's error, or over sufferings and afflictions, or because they were pleading for help to come to them from heaven. For a spiritual man does not [?] weep, because his joy is constant. If he does weep, he is moved by thoughts of the soul, as I said. So it was with Simon Cephas, who wept bitterly when he remembered how he had denied our Lord. Notice that wherever our Lord wept, the evangelist makes clear which thoughts made him weep. He wept over people when he came down to the level of their minds and saw their dead hearts. But when a person's mind is in the spirit, he does not weep, just as an angel does not weep. If weeping belonged to the spiritual way of life, then the righteous would weep without end in the kingdom, since there they are of the spirit. So there is no weeping in the spiritual way of life. Then what is the rank of someone who weeps all the time, as measured against spiritual growth? Only that of an infant who is always crying. An infant cries less and less as he grows toward full stature, until he reaches an age at which crying no longer suits him. In the same way, if God allows someone who is always weeping the tears of discernment to draw near to spiritual growth, then the more his mind grows in the spirit, the more he stops weeping

and comes to live in joy. But someone who has no feeling at all in his mind, and is not moved by compassion, compares to a spiritual person as an unborn child compares to someone of full bodily stature. The unborn child is wholly in the womb, and nothing of him is seen in this world. In the same way, a person who feels no compunction has his whole mind shut up here, and his thoughts never go out to another world. You had already raised this subject with me in another letter, but I felt obliged, for your benefit, to explain it to you as well, since you often do not come across that letter. What I have said about the cause of tears holds even where a person has a natural sensitivity. And the same distinctions of thought that I described for weeping are also what stir anyone's sighs. Now let me also explain the subject of love: what causes make it take root in bodily, soulish and spiritual people. Then everyone who considers what I say may know how far short they fall of true love. For I see that anyone at all imagines that he has acquired love. Yet the degree of human love lies below the degree of divine love, and unless a person first reaches the measure of love for people, he is not raised to the measure of love for God. As blessed John also said, “Whoever does not love his brother, whom he sees, cannot love God, whom he does not see” (1 John 4:20). So let me now set out the distinctions of love, and which thoughts nourish it in the soul. First, learn that God has set it in us by nature. If the soul's power could not be moved to love, we would not have been told, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deuteronomy 6:5). So in the bodily person

the love that belongs to his nature is stirred by these passions: desire and attachment. Desire grows out of thinking about the body, and the love of possessions grows out of the love of many desires. For whoever wants to be known in the world for power, honour and pride is the one in whom the love of wealth grows. And this love stirs him to love particular people, I mean those who obtain these things for him. That is why the love of bodily people is not true. It began to stir in their minds out of shifting wishes, and it rests on wishes that do not last. Clearly, when the things that caused their love change, their love changes with them. For their love began with beauty that fades, with wealth that perishes, and with power that comes to an end. Let us now turn to another rank, the soulish, in whom there is a love that is neither true nor false. I mean that it is not false for this reason: a person who is soulish in his way of life does not have a growing passion for wealth, nor a passion to do what his desire wants. So nothing leads him to love people, since he neither thirsts for wealth nor loves beauty. For that reason the passion of love is not really present in him. Even if he imagines that he loves people with divine love, he has not yet come near that measure. For the love of God is not acquired from the world of the body but from understanding his mysteries. And because he has not come near this, he falls short of loving all people. For perfect love is this: to love everyone in the likeness of God. And if the soulish person loves a particular individual, his love does not come from knowledge but from some cause that draws him to it. If his love were true, and he loved those he loves with knowledge, he would not hate the person who wrongs him. But if

he does hate, he should know that some cause drew him to hate, just as some cause drew him to love. Again, a person who is soulish in knowledge can love only someone who agrees with his teaching. Nor is this the love of truth. For the love of truth loves even those who do not agree with one's teaching, just as God loves even those who do not agree with his will. But the spiritual person perfectly acquires love for God and for people. He does not acquire it by chance, or because of anything visible, but from knowledge. Eutropius said: From what knowledge? John said: May our Lord reveal it to you, my beloved, for the causes of this love are beyond your hearing. Even if they were spoken, you would not be able to understand them. But I will mention some of them. True love is acquired from limpidity upward, and whoever is below limpidity has not yet reached up to its height. The gift of perfect love will be given to all human nature in the other world. For every gift a person receives from limpidity of soul upward belongs to the gifts that come after the resurrection. Since after the resurrection no one will hate his neighbour, is it not clear that true love is a gift of God? Let me also speak of another passion, zeal, and of the thoughts in which it arises in each of these ranks. In the bodily man, then, zeal is directed at these things: other people's power, the wealth of those richer than he is, and the life of those who live more comfortably than he does. All the passion of his zeal is stirred by envy, and his envy itself begins with the love of visible things. Eusebius said: And someone like this, by what means could he be delivered from these things?

John said: He could be freed from them by hoping for what is to come. If he considered how weak the things he envies are, and how strong the things that are promised are, he could not fail to be cleansed of this passion. Now that I have stated the cause of his sickness and the cause of his healing, let me turn to the soulish man and show where his zeal comes from, and what it is stirred against. In the soulish person zeal begins for this reason. Because he has risen above the evil deeds that are seen in the body, and has not perceived the things greater than himself, he thinks that what he has is perfection. And because everyone else falls short of him in visible deeds, he begins to be stirred to zeal and to find fault with their deeds. From the cause of his zeal he accumulates hatred. If he does not love worldly honours, his zeal does not come from envy but from what he takes to be a sense of righteousness. But if he loves honour, his zeal is stirred by envy. And the wretch does not know that just as he judges bodily people, so he is judged by spiritual ones. As the apostle said, he cannot know it, because it is judged spiritually (1 Corinthians 2:14). The passion I have described belongs to the one who is soulish in his way of life. But the zeal of one who is soulish in his knowledge arises for this reason. He has come close to the study of wisdom and has taken hold of an understanding of various things. Looking at his own diligence, he sees that everyone is beneath him. And because he has not perceived the mysteries greater than himself, he thinks that he knows the truth. So he begins to be zealous against those who do not agree with him, believing them to be in error. So Paul was zealous against the disciples, believing that he knew the truth and they were in error. In both these ranks, the thoughts of zeal go as far as murder, just as some of

the righteous were zealous for the destruction of people. So the zeal of the soulish and the bodily is bounded by these two aims: that of people who are soulish in wisdom and in conduct, and that of people who are bodily in mind and in deeds. But in the spiritual man there is no zeal for anyone's destruction. Our Lord not only showed no such zeal, but even rebuked his disciples for being carried away by zeal against the Samaritans. Eusebius said: What did he mean when he said to them, “You do not know what spirit you are of” (Luke 9:55)? John said: If they had known what measure of wisdom he had come to bring them to, they would not have been boiling with anger in such thoughts. In the same way, once they knew what knowledge they had received in the mystery of Christ, they not only rose above that frame of mind but were even made perfect in love for the wicked. As for the zeal of the spiritual man, if it is right to call it zeal, it is nothing other than this: he burns with divine zeal and with complete love for people to bring those who stray to the knowledge of the truth. This is what our Lord and his disciples did. Consider this point too. From the time a person begins to move away from evil deeds, he goes through many distinct states of mind, and then he comes near the soulish degree. And when he begins in turn to be purified of his inner thoughts, he goes through many more, and then he attains limpidity. From limpidity upward, it is a mystery without limit. There is a great deal to teach about the distinctions among these: how a person moves away from bodiliness and comes near soulishness, what distinctions there are between those who are bodily in conduct and those who are bodily in mind, and between those who are soulish in mind and those who are soulish in conduct. For just as there are many changes in the growth of the body, so

there are many changes in the growth of the mind. When a person is ten years old, his thoughts match his stature. At fifteen, his impulses are different. At twenty, others are added to them. And when he reaches thirty, the earlier ones are replaced by other thoughts. In the same way, the inner mind goes through many changes as it grows. Because this world is bodily, the measures of the body are known in it. But inner growth cannot be seen, except by someone who has separated himself from the body in his mind. Infants grow in the womb, and those in this world cannot see them growing. In the same way, inner minds grow, and their growth cannot be seen except in that world. When infants come out of their mother's womb, the stature of each one is seen in bodily form. In the same way, when we come out of this womb, the wide expanse of the earth, and appear in that world, the measure of mind to which each of us has grown will be revealed, whether in evil or in good. Since it would take a great deal to explain these changes, I will at least show by illustration from what point a person begins to love people. When the body completes the first stage, childhood, and enters the second, youth, it cannot help being stirred by desire for the pleasure that belongs to its world, which is the union of marriage. So too in the growth of the inner person. When he completes the first stage, infancy, which is carelessness about the fear of God, and enters the second stage, which is limpidity, he cannot help being stirred by the pleasure that belongs to his world, which is love for people. And as the body in its youth stands fully within its world, so this inner person stands in another world through love for

people. If I were to tell you everything in detail, you would see that it would run much longer than an account of the five books of the Law. These are seeds, and they may grow abundantly in you. What I say about the soulish rank leaves aside the case of someone who was previously caught up in the habits of his labour. Everyone who is soulish in mind is bodily in conduct, and everyone who is soulish in conduct is bodily in mind. The one rejoices in his labour, and the other takes pride in his wisdom. There is also another rank among people, in whom nothing is practised, either in secret or in the open, except the deeds of the flesh. And there are some who have begun to leave bodiliness behind but have not yet come near soulishness, and what their passions are is another subject. And there are some who have begun to rise above soulishness but have not reached the mind of the spirit, and speaking of their impulses is another matter. Nature is not to seek the spiritual way of life, because it lies beyond the nature that is given to people in the other world. In this life, God gives it only to whom he knows it is fitting. So it was with Paul, whom he brought to this measure together with the rest of the disciples. That is why no one is condemned for failing to reach this greatness. Eusebius said: Still, I think it would be childish, after hearing these things, not to take on the burden of praying constantly to be made worthy of them. John said: Let me now set out who are overcome by rancour and cannot truly be reconciled. Anger stirs in everyone, but in those who are of admirable nature not even these passions are strong. A person who suppresses his anger within himself through wisdom is not only free of rancour

but is close to overcoming the passion of anger itself. But a person who suppresses his anger, not through wisdom and for his own good, but silences it within himself by artifice, is a rancorous man. Let me also give the cause of his rancour. He has not been cleansed of anger enough to be patient with a calm mind. So, as someone who has not given his anger what it wants in blows or curses, its inner impulses then form rancour in him until the time comes for revenge. This kind of person is therefore reconciled only after a long time. Eusebius said: Then who is the person who is not held by rancour for long when he is angered? And what is the cause of the shortness of his rancour? John said: A person whose anger is sharp, and who is often carried away by it, does not stay rancorous for as long as the first one I described. Eusebius said: How so? John said: Because the impulses of his anger found relief and rest in pouring out words, his thoughts do not linger long in hidden resentment. In fact, he often even regrets what he did before. There are many other such things among those found in godless people, who never have their fill of harming their neighbours. For I am not speaking of demons but of human beings. Whoever does not restrain his envy and does not know reconciliation is not counted among human beings. Rather, as the Gospel teaches, he is counted among the angels of Satan, since he sends them with them into the Gehenna of fire. For if they had not resembled them, he would not have condemned them along with them, since God's judgement is not unjust. Let me also reveal the passion of malice, and the cause that makes it grow in the soul.

It is present in most people. But in people who are used to busying themselves with what others do, the passion of malice is strong. Eusebius said: By what means could their passion be lessened? John said: By not giving their minds free rein. When their minds stir them to wander in thought, they should restrain them, and not give their hidden impulses relief by pouring out words. When the mouth and nostrils are closed, what remains of a person's life ebbs away. In the same way, by keeping silent from talking about others, the inner passion withers. And once this passion has ceased, the passion of love enters. Their souls have no chance to be moved to love for people as long as this passion keeps sprouting in them. Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear. Hear also the opinion that others have held about the nature of the soul. They say that it is moved by three passions, namely discernment, love and anger. But they spoke very poorly about it, for animals too are moved by these three passions. Animals love their young, they grow angry at whoever harms them, and they know how to show loving regard for whoever feeds them. So the race of dogs knows how to tell its masters apart from strangers and love them, and “the ox knows its owner” (Isaiah 1:3), and there are many other such things. These three passions move the nature of the body. The first is love for the life that belongs to its nature, and the other two are born from this passion I have mentioned. Because the nature of the body is bound by love for its life, against anyone who opposes its life

it shows anger, and anyone who helps this passion, the love of its life, it knows how to honour. But the nature of the soul is far above these three passions, and in a human being it is only the body that is moved by them. As for the power of the soul's understanding, I have dealt with it briefly, according to the subject you set me. Peace.
The second: On the distinction between the passions of the soul, on the cause of their movements, and on which of them belong to its nature and which lie outside its nature.

When we had finished the midday service and gone in to him after the close of prayer, he began to speak to us: "My beloved, a helpful physician who cares about the pains of the body explains how they are to be healed. In the same way I too, so far as my smallness allows, have taken on the task of telling you not only what you asked but also other things you did not ask, so that anyone who cares to be taught in these matters may find in them healing for his hidden pains. Yet I know that few care about this teaching. Still, I will gladly also show the reason for their attitude: why they do not take care over the pains of the soul as they take care over the pains of the body. When this reason is understood, even those who excel in their way of life may be kept from anger, and not be enraged at those who do not care for the life of their souls. For it is from lack of knowledge that the righteous grow angry with sinners. If they knew with how much labour a person is made worthy to become a man of God in his deeds, they would acknowledge the goodness of God, by whose help they attained this measure, and toward sinners they would feel the pain of grief, not the anger of

zeal. The reason why a person takes care over the pain of his body is this: the whole of nature, in the course of its elements, serves the body and not the soul. So the body feels the comforts that are in it and the afflictions that come from it, and because its comforts and afflictions are visible in the body, a person is moved to take trouble over them." Eusebius said: "We have heard the reason you gave for why there is care for the pains of the body. But what is the reason that there is no care for the pains of the soul?" The Solitary said: "The nature of the soul is subtler than any body, and its life springs from a life exalted above the body, since even after its separation from the body it endures in the life of its nature. For this reason its pains are not visible to people, nor the causes by which it is struck, and the remedies that heal them cannot be perceived by the senses. It is not cured by physicians' poultices, nor helped by a mixture of roots. But God, who knows the causes of the soul's injuries, which come from evil deeds, forbade those deeds in his tablets: 'You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness against your neighbour' (Deut. 5:17 ff.), and the rest, that they should not covet one another's goods. So that by refraining from these things, which are done in the body, people might also keep their inner movements at rest. But since people were in agreement neither with the good nature within them nor with the commandment of the Lord of all, for this reason, their disobedience, they set about every evil. Their knowledge was changed into error, and their inner self was corrupted with blemishes. So that, as it were, they could neither see nor hear, but were like the dead, who feel nothing, in the loves of their inner selves. And while in the sickness of this

mind people remain, and the greater part of their impulses is swept away in the love of glory." Eusebius said: "You have spoken very profoundly and truly about the passions, their causes and the healing of their blemishes. Anyone who took the trouble to understand these things would truly become a man of God in his mind. But since your discourse has reached this passion of the love of glory, we want to know from what cause it begins." The Solitary said: "This passion begins from boasting, and boasting begins from a foolish mind, and folly from not knowing this life. People do not understand the weakness of their affairs or the emptiness of the glory that comes from them. They are not wise about the wonder of God's works and the wisdom of his governance, nor about the meanness of human nature: that even as people blaze up they cool down, even as they rule they are dissolved, even as they are exalted they are brought low; that the order of their nature stands in constant change, and all their deeds are subject to dissolution. And because they do not reflect on these things, they are stolen away into the love of praise from one another. Above all, a person does not stop to say: 'What is this vanity that has gripped me, that the eyes of men matter more to me than the eyes of God, and I long for their praise and not for the praise that comes from God? As if their glory were higher to me than the glory of the Lord of all, and the honour that comes from men equal to me with the honour of angels! Woe is me, a man! God created me free, yet I have placed myself under the lordship of many, since I am a slave to everyone in trying to please everyone. As if Christ paid out the glory of men! As if

people were the tribunal that rewards my deeds!' If a person's mind held steadily to these thoughts, the passion of the love of praise would not dwell in him. For these impulses are the enemies of this passion. When many people live in a house in the peace of a single mind, their enemy cannot get in to them for fear of them; in the same way this passion is driven off by the united agreement of these inner thoughts. But when a man's mind is emptied of these impulses, first he becomes lacking in understanding; then distinguished in his deeds; then proud; then a lover of boasting; then a lover of praise. And from the love of glory he goes on to envy. Envy is not born of wickedness in everyone; it arises from various passions. In boastful people envy does not spring from wickedness, as others have said, but from vainglory, as Paul said: 'Do not be vainglorious, envying one another' (Gal. 5:26). But in those who have no love of praise, envy is born of wickedness, and the cause of its growth is that they cannot bear to look on the honour of others. Among craftsmen, or judges' assessors, or judges, or wise men, envy of one another comes from the love of praise: since each of them wants to be praised himself, he envies his fellow his reputation. But other people in general envy one another out of wickedness. The poor, for instance, do not envy one another in order to be praised; their envy of one another is over collecting a larger gift. This kind of person, who loves glory in the praise of visible deeds, does not have much wickedness in him.

Eusebius said: "Why is it that wickedness abounds in others, but in this one it is slight?" The Solitary said: "Because the lover of glory is lavish with his gifts. And because he looks to be praised by everyone, the passion of wickedness finds no room in his boastful impulses. Indeed, he often even begins to do good, and through the passion of goodness he puts an end to the passion of wickedness. Yet his goodness does not reach out to everyone, for that belongs to the mercy that resembles God. His goodness is confined to those who praise him, like judges, generals and magnates, who throw their wealth into the theatre for people to look at. That they do not give to the poor is not from wickedness but because righteousness counts for little with them. For the passion of wickedness, as I said, loses its savour through the love of glory. But whoever does not love to be praised for the splendour of the world's affairs, and also does not give to the poor from what he has, that kind has much wickedness in him, and his wickedness strips him of mercy. As for that first order, the one praised in the world, the love of praise from men becomes the reason that he is not merciful to the weak. Because he is enslaved to praise for affairs, he does not turn toward the more excellent praise of a noble gift. But I will tell you what calls everyone to mercy. Whoever is not merciful can become merciful in this way: by forcing his mind even when he is unwilling, and training himself to give to the needy, so that through the constancy of his giving abundant mercy may be continually in his soul. And whoever lacks the means to drive wickedness out of himself by giving and so become merciful can become merciful in this way: by forcing his mind even when he does not wish to, forgiving those who wrong him, and not letting himself be drawn into repaying evils. As for the passion of anger

in this kind of person, who wants to be praised for the splendour of affairs: when he grows angry, his anger is not born of the wickedness of envy but of boasting. For boasting is one thing and vainglory another. Pride clings to boasting, and haughtiness to vainglory. Again, the passion that begets haughtiness is one thing, and the one that begets pride is another. From pride hatred is born, when the proud man is angered; from haughtiness comes contempt for people. So when the mind is haughty it is angry as if with contempt, while the mind of the proud man is angry as if with hatred. When the proud man humbles someone, he humbles him out of the hatred of wickedness; but the haughty-minded man does it because he despises people and counts them as nothing. These passions in turn have a cause, and their cause has yet another cause. Without recounting all of them, what they are and why they differ: if a person knows them, he can avoid being caught by them; and if he is caught because he did not know about them all beforehand, he can easily escape such causes by understanding their causes. The beginning and cause of all hateful causes is what I said above: that people are not wise about the weakness of their nature and the changeableness of their affairs. But since not everyone is of one mind in the love of glory, I will show the distinctions within this passion, not all of them, but at least three variations in it, and how it appears differently in different people. Those who love to be praised for setting the world's affairs in order and for being greeted with the bows of honour have haughtiness in their love of [?]. But those who want to be praised for good deeds are proud in mind." Eusebius said: "And why, when both of them have the passion

of glory, are they distinguished from one another by these two passions, so that one is haughty and the other proud? If the same passion moves in them, how is it that they do not agree in these others?" The Solitary said: "They are not alike in these other passions because the cause of the love of glory is not the same in one who has abundant power to establish affairs and in one who wants to be praised for good deeds. And because their cause differs, these passions are also found in them differently. In those who hold power, power lifts up their mind, and because many are subject to them, it raises their mind above those under their hand. And because not everyone can do the things they do by their power and by the wealth they possess, their heart is lifted up for this reason too. But in those who are praised for good deeds, the passion of pride creeps in whenever they see that their deeds are known. That is why our Lord, who knew the cause of their pride, that it comes from being seen by people, commanded them to hide their good deeds from people's sight, saying: 'Do not do your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them' (Matt. 6:1). This order of people, who want to be praised for good deeds and wish to be honoured in people's eyes through deeds that are thought good, is more cunning about human thoughts than the first order I mentioned. The first, who want to boast in the affairs of setting the world in order, know nothing of the wisdom of craftiness, and are even very foolish about the passions of men. The reason for their folly is this: they have no care for the good order of cities for the sake of duty, but only to be praised, and so their mind is confined

to these thoughts, and they remain uncultivated about human minds. If their power and wealth were taken from them, they would differ in no way from the animals in knowledge. But those who care for setting in order the places of the afflicted, not to be praised but to help, have room in their mind to become wise in other good things too. Now that these two orders have been discussed, which, though both subject to the love of praise, differ in other passions, I will speak about another order of people: those who love to be praised neither for the splendour of the world nor for excellent deeds, but want only to please people by their power. People of this sort become like-minded with every mind, and their enmity is not easily detected, because they speak to each person according to what pleases his mind. They make great use of the pose of humility in people's eyes, as Absalom did before the people. Because he wanted to be praised for his power, he put on the guise of humility and spoke to each person according to what the listener had in mind. This kind, who want only to please by their power, go deeper in sharp cunning than the two orders I mentioned. And since I have spoken about their agreement in the love of praise and the various differences in their impulses, I will say in which passion, again, they agree. All three of the orders I mentioned, whenever something is said about them that disgraces them in people's eyes, in front of someone who hears it, are not at first kindled to anger. They are struck instead with the passion of distress, like someone whose beloved possession has met with opposition, and then from the distress they are stirred, in turn, to anger. That is the first order, which boasts in the splendour of affairs. But the one who

is praised for good deeds is dragged by distress more than the first. And his distress turns toward enmity against the one who brings him disgrace. But the one who wants to please people with his power under the guise of humility, when he hears that someone has spoken ill of him, does not turn to hatred or anger; he swallows his feelings with great distress. These three orders of lovers of praise, then, agree in feeling distress when they are disgraced, but they do not agree in the other passions. Whoever is not a lover of praise, however, is filled with the impulse of anger whenever he meets a slight in word or deed, becoming a hater and a reviler. For anger begets cursing." Eusebius said: "And why is it that the one who wants to please by his power under the guise of humility is not stirred to anger when he hears that someone has spoken ill of him?" The Solitary said: "Because the love of glory does not allow him. Through the humility he displays he wants to please by his power, and he does not want to be seen as hot-tempered, lest he be disgraced still more." Eusebius said: "But look, the first order you mentioned, who want to be praised for their affairs, are lovers of praise too, and when they hear something that disgraces them, though they are struck with distress, they are still stirred to anger. How is it that the passion of the love of praise does not keep them from being seen as angry?" The Solitary said: "Because they do not seek praise under the guise of humility, such that, if they appeared hot-tempered, they would be disgraced." Eusebius said: "You have put it very well." The Solitary said: "Let me tell you another point as well: which of these three orders of people has a struggle to be delivered from the passion of the love of glory, so as to do nothing in order to please people.

Know that those who boast in the splendour of the world have no way of having a struggle." Eusebius said: "That runs contrary to their nature. When their nature praises humility, how can they have no struggle against vainglory?" The Solitary said: "Because their mind is captive to the things we have described, and they do not reflect on the changeableness in which human nature stands. And because their mind is imprisoned in the things people see, their thinking does not leave the place of the love of praise. Even the part of their nature that praises humility has been hidden by it, so that it is not recognized in them, though they do praise those who are humble." Eutropius said: "And how is it that, though they praise humility, it is not seen in them?" The Solitary said: "Because the good nature in them cannot help showing its power, bearing witness in their mind to the beauty of gentleness. But because the passions of haughtiness, boasting and the love of praise have multiplied in them, the power of humility in their nature is not seen in them on account of the great number of these. First, because the good will does not support this passion of humility; and second, because all the affairs that accompany such a person, namely power, wealth, freedom of speech and honour, strengthen this passion of the love of praise with their help. So the power of humility has stopped struggling against them, and hands over the inner members to the will of those passions. And man's will itself gives them as dwellings to those passions, so that they may dwell in them with their impulses. But the passion of humility goes down and stands in the depths of the soul's understanding as its nature, so that in its own place it may show

its power, by praising the excellence of humility, showing its will in the nature of the soul by praising and commending humility. And because a person's will did not help the passion of humility by giving it a place to dwell in the members of the body, humility is not seen in that person; the will of the body empties him of it, along with all its conduct. In that natural will of the soul the power of humility lies hidden, and it shows its power in this, that it does not despise humility. But its power is not seen in that person, because it has been driven out of him by the will of the body." Eutropius said: "You have spoken very powerfully. But now that you have shown that one who loves power cannot be delivered from vainglory, explain to us who it is that grieves that the passion of the love of praise overcomes him, and has a struggle against it so as not to be enslaved to it." The Solitary said: "The one who wants to be praised for good deeds has a struggle from time to time over his good deeds, so that they may not be done for the sake of glory from people. For whenever he wants to do a good deed, along with the thought of wanting it the passion of human praise creeps into him. When he does the good deed, he does it for the sake of glory, for he has not yet been freed so as to do it purely, without this passion. And when he is about to leave undone the good deed he intended, he falls into struggle, because he wants to give up the good deed he had intended. In these considerations he arrives at one of two things: either he completes the good deeds he wanted to do, or he does away with them altogether. This, then, is the struggle into which the mind falls of one who devotes himself to good deeds and wants to look to the aim of pleasing God and not men. But I counsel such a person not to hold back from

doing good, even if his good deeds look to the aim of pleasing people. For no one gains anything when good deeds stop, but everyone is helped when good deeds are done." Eusebius said: "And why does this one who wants to do good have a struggle against vainglory?" The Solitary said: "Because his mind is in the middle: it looks both toward the promises and toward people. Because he wants to find mercy at the judgment, he wants to do good to the needy. Because he is not perfected in love for people, so as to do good to them out of love for them, his mind rejoices at being praised by them. And because he fears the judgment, when his mind convicts him that he does not do his good deeds purely, without regard for human praise, he falls into struggle and grief. But I, my beloved, did not wish only to list the names of these passions, what they are, how they are, and what makes them grow, but also their healing: by what thoughts each of them is healed. This I have shown as far as I was able. But since many other matters lie before our eyes, I will say nothing about them. For we cannot recount all the causes of each of the passions: what they are, from what cause they are stirred in people, the order of their growth, and which impulses sustain them. One could, for instance, speak about the diversity of human opinions, and how many have held views about them. Some have made the passions natural, holding that the cause of their strength lies in nature itself, in the order of the body's temperament. Others attributed them to the cause of evil that was mixed into nature. Others called them demons who dwell in the inner man, and they say that these grow stronger in a person than other causes. Some hold

that these passions belong to the soul, and that the soul is their cause. But to argue against each of these opinions is not the aim we have set ourselves: which of them spoke better than the others, or whether all of them alike strayed from the truth. There are also other matters we have not yet discussed: simplicity, the middle state, and the excellence of exalted knowledge. Simplicity, because many live in innocence. The middle state, because many do not stand in innocence and have not reached exalted knowledge, but are in between: they are far from innocence and have not reached exalted wisdom. Most of the world is in this middle order. They do not walk innocently or practise simplicity in their conduct, nor have they risen to the spiritual wisdom by which they would excel in knowledge with all simplicity. The whole middle order is crafty in its conduct, wicked in its deeds and cunning in its thoughts, along with every other hateful thing. But I say that it helps a person greatly, if he is not worthy of excellent wisdom, not to abandon the first order of innocence. Otherwise, having left his first simplicity without reaching glorious knowledge, he may end up in the middle order, which is wholly occupied with sharp cunning. If a man leaves his house to go to the city and never enters the city, it would have been better for him not to have left his house than to be stuck on the road. In the same way it helps a person to be innocent without knowledge rather than to abandon innocence and never draw near to the wisdom that would make him knowing in all simplicity. True innocence is found in knowledge. For there is no innocence that is ignorance without folly mixed

into it. It is by this knowledge, which is higher than ordinary innocence and than the whole cunning middle state, that what our Lord said is fulfilled in a person: 'Be innocent as doves and wise as serpents' (Matt. 10:16)." Eusebius said: "What sort of people are those who stand in the middle order?" The Solitary said: "Judges, judges' assessors and the educated, if they do not draw near to excellence." Eusebius said: "How, then, is the shrewdness of the serpent to be found in a person?" The Solitary said: "Our Lord gave us an understanding of this in the illustration of the serpent's shrewdness. The serpent knows that it cannot shed its old skin in a wide place. But when it makes itself enter a narrow place and fine cracks, and then, stretching its body and squeezing itself thin with effort, presses to get out, its old skin catches in the cracks and it comes out renewed, leaving its skin behind. So we too, by treading the path of afflictions and by the labour of a patient mind, should strip from the inner man all the conduct of the old man. Then, having stripped off all that is old, his departure from the body will be in all purity. Let us also leave aside another order we might have discussed: most people are inclined to recount the evil deeds of others and not their good ones. When someone hears of many good deeds by a person, they do not stick in his mind, nor does it occur to him to tell of them. But if he hears one hateful thing about him, look, he runs, look, he hurries to tell it to everyone he meets, even when no one asks. As for the good deeds, even when called upon, he finds it distasteful to tell them. The things that would

profit those who hear them he keeps quiet about, and what harms everyone who hears it he tells." Eusebius said: "What shall we say about these people? There is much wickedness in them, and it leaves no room for good to take hold in them. Yet we see that there are excellent people who enjoy telling of the good deeds of others, but do not even wish to hear anything disgraceful." The Solitary said: "The cause of these traits is not only the temperaments of the body, nor is it the cause of evil. Some have grown used to them from the habits of their upbringing; some from lack of training in good deeds; some, because they do not care to keep people from stumbling, do not restrain talk that harms them; some from lack of concern for their own souls." Eusebius said: "If that concern is in them, why are they not concerned?" The Solitary said: "Concern has indeed been placed in all people. But each person is concerned with what he has come to love and with what first took hold of him. For no one is without concern: each is concerned with whatever he wants to be concerned with. And to show you that causes outside us arouse these passions in us: there is a man who is captive to vainglory through his wealth and power. If his wealth and power are taken from him, his passion also ceases, and this passion no longer lives in him. The cause of his power aroused it in him, and the cause of his power's ending quieted it in him." Eusebius said: "Do these passions belong by nature to the soul, or to the body, and are they aroused in a person by various causes? Since there are wise men who have distinguished which belong to the body and which

to the soul, I want to be assured whether they spoke truly, or whether there is anything good in what they said that my soul should hold to." The Solitary said: "Set out which ones they assigned to the body and which to the soul." Eusebius said: "They say that these belong to the body: sleep, hunger, thirst, desire and dissoluteness. And these, they say, belong to the soul: anger, zeal, discernment, envy, love of power, haughtiness, boasting and love." The Solitary said: "Those of the body are indeed as you said. But the ones attributed to the soul are not its passions by nature. Rather, on account of the affairs to which the body is bound by its need and love for them, room is made for these passions in the mind. Tell me, what does envy come from? Is it not from this: that a person loves something, and sees another who surpasses him in it, whether in wealth, or power, or beauty, or skill, or in being known to the great? Whatever a person loves and sees another honoured for, he envies him. Now this power or wealth or skill or beauty, or being known to the great, what caused these things to be loved and envied: the body's need for them or the soul's?" Eusebius said: "The body's need. The soul has no need of wealth, nor of bodily beauty, nor of power. What would the nature of the soul gain from a person's ruling over people? Power too is something seen in the body." The Solitary said: "If it is the body's need for these things that made them loved, then it turns out that the love of affairs is the cause of envy in the one who loves them."

Eusebius said: "If the love of affairs is the cause of these passions, how do they gain power over the soul, when, as you said, they are outside its nature? And if they have no kinship with the soul, how has something outside the soul's nature gained power over it?" The Solitary said: "In the same way that stains and wounds appear in the body from a cause outside it." Eusebius said: "They are not outside it. It was harmed by something that struck its nature." The Solitary said: "Even though it was struck by something that struck its nature, these scars are still outside its health, since at any time they are able to pass away. Or again: when a person turns toward sleep, he sees images outside himself. They are not in him, but because he has turned toward them, fear of them takes hold of him. Then, when he wakes and turns from them to look at himself, little by little those images fade from his memory, his fear of them is taken away, and he returns to his former state, no longer remembering them or fearing them. In the same way, when the nature of the soul turns toward the body, the passions and impulses of the body, though they are not in the soul's own nature, gain power over it and harm it. But when a person turns his gaze away from the body toward his soul, and does not turn toward the body's desires for a long time, turning instead to his soul through good deeds, little by little these passions die out, and he stands purely in the order of his nature." Eusebius said: "You have given a very helpful illustration of this. But since you have said that affairs and the body are the cause of these passions, we see that the order of demons neither needs our affairs nor is clothed with a body. And though free of these things, in these passions

evil passions: by envy, by wickedness and by the love of power. The Solitary said: It would be another matter to speak about the nature of the demons. But since you have brought them in to demonstrate something about souls, show me any among them who desire what is fair and praise what is good, as there are among human beings. Eusebius said: Those human beings, too, conduct themselves fairly only when the nature of their souls is free from these passions. The Solitary said: Even if people do not do good things, yet the whole of human nature praises good things. By this the fair power of the soul is known: it is the one that praises good things. And because people are bound by love of their body's desires, they keep the goodness of their nature from being seen in them. But in the race of the demons you have not shown me even one who praises good things, so that I might be persuaded by the nature of the demons about what it shows of souls. For see, the whole nature of souls agrees with good things, since it praises good things, just as the whole will of the demons agrees with evil. Eusebius said: If the nature of the demons is not acceptable as a demonstration about souls, namely that it is not the body that makes them be moved by these passions but that by their very nature they incline toward them, then I bring forward the demonstration of the angels. When the angel Gabriel was sent by God's command to Zechariah the priest, he showed the passion of zeal and of anger. For he was angry that the priest's mind was divided about the promise of his word, and in zeal he put a muzzle on his mouth. The Solitary said: This zeal and anger of his: were these things said of him while he was in the order of his own nature and standing in his own world, or when he came into our world and appeared in our likeness? If it was when he came into our world and appeared in our likeness that he was said to have done them, then you should not attribute

something that came from his activity to the order of his nature. For if you think that these passions belong to his nature because he was angry and zealous, then the compound sounds heard from that compound form would also be natural to him. But if the form in which he appeared was ours and not his nature's, and the voice in which he spoke belonged to our nature and not to his spirituality, then the passion of zeal he showed Zechariah in response to the division of his mind was also a passion of ours and not of his. The blessed Apostle did not attribute these passions to the nature of the soul but to the body. For he says in the Epistle to the Galatians: "The fruits of the flesh are fornication, impurity, lewdness, sorcery, enmity, strife, zeal, anger, contention, divisions, factions, envy, murder, drunkenness, revelry, and everything like these" (Gal. 5:19ff). If these are its fruits, and he did not count among them love, or humility, or kindness, or any of the good passions, then to whom should we think these praiseworthy passions of love and virtue belong? If to the body, see, they are not in it apart from the good will of the soul. For when the soul turns from the side of the body toward virtue, it makes its virtue shine out in the sight of the body's conduct. And if they do not belong to the soul by nature, what is the cause of those good passions? Eusebius said: Are there, then, two wills in a human being? The Solitary said: There is one of the body and another of the soul. Otherwise, which will was it that God, through the prophet, censured in the people of Israel: "They went after the will of their heart" (Jer. 9:13)? For see, the fair nature in them praises good things. And the blessed Paul said to the Galatians: "so that you do not do what you wish" (Gal. 5:17). If there were only one will in our nature, we could not wish

not to do what we wish. And what is the will that wishes in us that we not do what we wish, if not the one that urges [?] us to set aside the will of the body, so that, through the good will of the soul, we do not do the will of the body that is in us? For you ought to know this: if the soul by its nature inclines toward these evil passions, then they belong to its nature. And if they belong to its nature, it cannot be free of being moved by them, not even after it departs from the body.
