For just as the body sleeps because sleep is of its nature, eats because it hungers by nature, and drinks because it thirsts by nature, and these things are with it constantly, so too the soul would incline toward these passions at all times, if they were in its nature. And if they were of its nature, no one would be blamed for doing what is of his nature. For just as a person is not blamed for sleeping, since sleep is of his nature, nor for eating, since hunger is of his nature, nor for joining in intercourse, since desire is of his nature, so too, if he were envious or proud, he would not be condemned at the judgment for having these things, since they would be of his nature. But these passions are condemned by God; he constantly commands that they should not exist, and he puts a muzzle on whoever is enslaved to them. Together with the other things I said above, this shows that the nature of the soul is free from these passions, and that they gain power over the mind through causes outside the body and through the body. We also see that these passions do not stir only in human beings, but also in the other bodies that have no soul. For we find that the nature of beasts, birds, creeping things and the fish in the sea is moved by these passions: by anger, by wickedness, by love, by desire, by discernment and by pride.

For birds have discernment according to their nature, and a love that makes them cling to their young. We find wickedness in beasts and creeping things. The race of dogs is wrathful and discerning: it barks angrily at strangers, and it discerns how to honor its masters more than strangers. And in the race of horses we find that they walk proudly. Yet these passions are not stirred in these bodies by a soul, since their soul is only their blood, and the excellent nature of the soul is not in them. But if you want to distinguish the passions, we find three distinctions in a human being: one belonging to the nature of the soul, another to its activity through the body, and a third to the body itself. To the nature of the soul belong knowledge and divine love. To the soul's activity in the body belong fair works. For fair conduct is the soul's activity in this life, since the nature of the soul is higher even than fair conduct. Good works, after all, are carried out through the body: mercy toward the weak, chastity, holiness, along with the rest of virtue. For if fair works belonged to the nature of the soul and not to its activity in the body, how would those good works cease in the new life? For the conduct of the new life is higher than chastity, than giving to the poor, than hospitality, than enduring afflictions, than not wronging others, and than being forbearing and bearing the burden of those who hate us. These are the works we are required to do in this life. But when the change comes to our body at the resurrection, we are raised even above works, so that in place of the conduct of works there will be the conduct of knowledge. Again, we find that there is an envy that belongs to evil and an emulation that belongs to good: "Do not be envious of one another" (Gal. 5:26). And again he says: "It is good to be emulous in what is good" (Gal. 4:18). This

is a good emulation. Which of these two, envy or emulation, are we to say belongs to the nature of the soul? For see, its spiritual nature is higher even than emulation in what is good; emulation in what is good is rather the soul's activity. And so that you may know that the nature of the soul is hidden from the members of the body in the depth of its mind, while in its activity in the body it is moved through the body's senses, consider this: when an injury occurs in one of the inner members, whether in the brain or in the heart, it is not the nature of the soul that is injured, but its activity in those members. For when a string on a lyre or a musical pipe is damaged, it is not the finger that plays it that is damaged; rather, the activity of the finger's art is prevented from becoming known through the instruments, the lyre or the pipe. And because the instruments through which the art used to be heard have been damaged, the activity of the hand also falls silent in them, though the art has not departed from the hand, nor has the hand been injured. So too the knowledge of the soul is kept safe in its nature, while its activity serves in the members. For if the nature of the soul were revealed in the body, it could even utter speech that is not composed of sounds. Eusebius said: But these virtues of the soul, namely love, affection, humility, gentleness, compassion and mercy, are not seen in everyone. The Solitary said: They are in all human beings, and there is no one who does not love and praise them. But the power to practice them is not seen in each person because of the many causes that keep that excellent activity from being seen in the body. For just as the sun, when it rises, is hidden from our sight if there is a thick mass of clouds and mists in the air, since they block its light, so habits

and the bad upbringing in which a person is raised block the virtue of his soul, so that it is not seen in him. And just as, when clouds and mists are rolled away from between us and it, the sun's rising is seen fully upon the earth, so, if evil habits are removed from a person, the whole virtue of the soul is seen fully in him. And just as the higher the sun climbs into the sky, the more the shadows of bodies shrink under its strong light, so the more the soul is revealed in the body through its virtue, the more the shadows of erring thoughts fade away under the light of the glorious mind. For this reason, my beloved, let us ask God at all times to make the light of his knowledge rise in us, so that the virtues he placed in us when he created our soul may appear to us. And as far as you are able, my beloved, do not grow slack in the labor of study. For if there is no knowledge, our whole inner being is darkness. But through study our mind, too, is gathered into itself. And because recounting them will profit you, I will tell you some stories about various people. There was a certain sage who, so as not to be hindered from study, declined to live inside the city and built himself a hut outside the wall. Beside it there was a field sown with wheat, and he passed by it constantly. When one of the people of his city asked him whether its crop was doing well, he said: "I do not even know whether it has been sown." See how profitable a love of study is for the soul: through its constant occupation with study it does not let the mind wander outside itself. I myself, too, saw with my own eyes a man who lived among two hundred people, and because he did not let his mind wander, as the story about him goes, for more than twelve years he did not know

who stood next to him in the row. Another sage, when there was turmoil in his city and he was not disturbed by it, was asked by someone: "Why is it that everyone is agitated, while you are calm?" He gave this answer: "How many times have I seen turmoil like this, even in a dream! Those who are agitated are right to be agitated, because they think they are standing in reality. But I am in the world of a dream, and I see a dream instead of the truth." The one who had asked him answered: "Then you ought to be agitated, since you are seeing a dream; for dreams agitate everyone." He answered: "I would be agitated if I did not know that I am seeing a dream. For whatever people are agitated about, it is because they think they are seeing the truth in the world. And whatever a person is agitated about in his dreams, it is because he thinks he is seeing the truth. But the true awakening of the resurrection is coming, and everyone will realize that he was in the world as if in a dream." A certain man, when he was insulted in a shameful way, did not take offense, but picked up a mirror. As he was looking into it, one of the bystanders said to him: "Why are you looking into it?" He said: "If my face really is as the man who insulted me said, it is not right for me to be angry, because he spoke the truth. And if what he said is not true, I have no need to take offense, because I am not as he said, and the deed does not follow the name." A certain judge, when he was told, "People call you a statue," answered: "And who will grant me never to show partiality?" A certain well-known man had been urging someone under his authority for ten years about some foolish desires, and he had not been persuaded, yet he still bore with him in kindness. One of his friends said to him: "I am amazed at you, that you have not become angry with him, since in all this long persuasion he has not obeyed you."

That man said to him: "Do not be amazed that I have been patient with him. For more than fifty years God has been urging me by his commandments to obey him, and I have still not obeyed him and done his will, yet he in his kindness has borne with me. And if I have not obeyed God, are you amazed that a man has not obeyed me, or that I have been patient for ten years and have not become angry with a man like myself?" One of the saints was struck so hard that his leg was broken, and someone else, seeing that he was not angry with the man who had struck him, said to him: "How is it that, when he dealt you such a blow, you did not become angry?" The saint said to him: "Even if I were walking along the road, how many times would something like this happen to me by stumbling on a stone? So now I reckon that it was a stone, and I stumbled on it against my will." A certain solitary, when his disciple broke the vessel he used to drink from and thought he would be angry with him, because he had no other vessel, answered his disciple and said: "Do not be troubled about this, for it was not something unbreakable that has been broken. It was always waiting for this." A certain soldier was a veteran in his service, and another younger than he was honored with a place above him in the ranks. When they saw that he was neither angry nor envious, he said to those who wondered at him: "Even if his body stands above me, my mind can still be above him. And see, even the roof-beam [?] of the palace stands above all of us, and we do not envy it. So let us not envy one another in bodily things. But in this, if one of us is greater than his fellow in wisdom, let us not hate him, but emulate him, so as to grow strong in it." Another soldier was boasting before a philosopher of his years of service, and the philosopher said to him: "You have been a soldier

for so many years. But for how long have you been wise?" One of the brothers told one of the saints that he had been in the clergy for forty years. The saint said to him: "I too have seen a man who had been called a merchant for forty years, and yet he could not get his daily bread without borrowing." Another man was boasting that for thirty years no meat had entered his mouth. That blessed man said to him: "For thirty years no meat has entered your mouth; but for how long has no curse come out of your mouth? What you were not commanded, you have kept for thirty years; but what you were commanded with every warning, have you kept it even for a week?" A certain blessed man lived among many brothers and had spent many years in his monastery. When one of those who were his juniors in discipleship took vessels better than his own, and his brothers told him, "So-and-so has taken vessels better than yours," he said: "The one who took them is also my own member. And just as, if the right hand is clothed and the left is bare, the left is not angry with the one that is clothed, so it is not fitting for us to be troubled at or envy the comfort of others. For if I had taken them, perhaps he would have been in want. And if our Lord accepted affliction upon himself for our relief, are we to seek a comfort that afflicts others?" When a certain sage's possessions were plundered, and he remained without anger and without making any claim, the man who had plundered him said: "Why are you not angry with me?" He said: "I have counted you as death. When death takes everyone away from his possessions, no one is angry with it." These things, my beloved, I have told because of the simplicity of these brothers of ours who have been received among us, who did not fully understand what was said earlier. So that their good will may not be wronged, I wanted to profit their minds through stories

of sayings told about these people. May God grant to all of us that our soul be trained in every virtue. And to him be glory for ever, amen. Here ends the second discourse: on the distinction of the passions of the soul, on the cause of their movements, and on which belong to its nature and which are outside its nature.
Again: The Third Discourse

Another time, when we had gone in to him and prayed, he began to say to us: "My beloved, do not be wearied by hearing the matter again. I want you to understand these things clearly, so I am compelled to repeat the point, and I urge you in your love to grasp it. Every person who is below the limpidity of the soul has no true love that does not stumble. Nor does he have the joy that springs up in the Spirit, which is not known from the body but is hidden in the understanding of the mind. Nor again does he have the means to perceive the knowledge of the mysteries of the other world, except with great toil and by bearing many burdens, and only if he first desires to be purified of these passions. For these passions, my beloved, are the blindness of the mind, while the limpidity of the soul is the light of its knowledge. No one knows the mystery of names simply by hearing them. This is true not only of spiritual mystery but also of the names used in any other branch of learning. Everyone hears the names of roots, and of 'hot' and 'cold', but what the power of these names of roots is, only someone who has learned the science of medicine knows. In the wisdom of the Chaldeans, too, the names of the stars and the signs of the regions are spoken of, yet not everyone who hears them knows, just by hearing, what the mystery of these names is. So also in this wisdom of Christ we know only the naming. For see, we hear many beautiful sayings

of wisdom from Paul, who said of God the Father, 'in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge' (Col 2:3). We hear the names of the treasures, but we do not know what their mystery is. And when someone says 'the treasures of the other world', that does not mean he says what they are. Again, when Paul, rich in knowledge, says, 'We speak wisdom among the perfect', and explains, 'wisdom not of this world' (1 Cor 2:6), he said that it exists, but he did not explain how it exists or in what mysteries. Nor again, when he says that we receive knowledge, did he say what that knowledge is, or in what mysteries it springs up. From such sayings the hearer may suppose that whenever speech looks toward the other world and talks about it, he already knows the knowledge of these things simply by hearing the words spoken about it. But if a person comes to be above the limpidity of the soul, not only is he able to understand the words of the new life, he also comes near to God through the revelation of the mysteries. For when someone stands above limpidity in his mind, Christ reveals himself to him. But to anyone who is below limpidity, Christ is not revealed in his knowledge. As I showed above from the evidence of the Gospel: 'Whoever has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me. And whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and show myself to him' (John 14:21). This is the way that brings one near to God; this is the path by which a person travels toward Christ. The mystery of Christ is to be revealed to the saints in the new world, and their conduct after the resurrection is above the limpidity of the soul, for it is the conduct of the mind that shares with God in his knowledge. For this reason a person cannot receive the revelation of Christ in this life unless he obeys his commandments. For it is through obedience to his commandments that

the purity of the mind comes. And if anyone disputes these things, all people bear witness to them. Of all who are confused and troubled and divided in mind and evil in their deeds, to whom has Christ been revealed in the knowledge of his mystery? And who has given himself to subjecting himself to the law of Christ in all humility of mind, and his mind was not enlightened in the hope of God? And who has taken care to purify his mind from evils, and his soul did not rejoice in God? If someone draws near to the toil of learning, he can come to know many things from people who have received a gift from God."

Eutropius said: "But see, there are many who toil at their ways of life and yet do not have the wisdom of understanding."

The Solitary said: "And what is better than this, that they have cast the desires of the body away from them? For if they are pure of the inner passions as well, they are truly filled with joy in the good mind of their hope. Since you have come to this matter, I want to show in my discourse what this toilsome way of life is, and for what reason it arises in each person. First, know that this toil is neither bodily nor soulish. It is not bodily, because it does not consist in the evils of the body. It is not soulish, because it does not do away with the inner passions; nor does the nature of the soul profit from these labours. Now that I have said what its rank is, hear what its cause is. This toil, then, consists of standing on the feet, keeping the eyes awake, going barefoot without shoes, and fasting from food, along with other afflictions. These do not come from knowledge but from the fervour of the mind. Fervour begins to arise in the mind from what grace has given it: the perception that there is another hope. And out of fear of the torment of Gehenna it begins to take pleasure in these things and to love what has been promised. For this reason

the mind grows fervent to afflict its body. It afflicts its body because of the thoughts I have described: pondering the torment to come, it seeks by afflicting its body here to be delivered from that torment. This toil is not carried by knowledge but by the fervour of a person's love. If his fervour happens to slacken, he begins to grow lax in his toil. And if the fervour is stripped from his mind and yet he does not change from his toil, then it is no longer out of love that he endures it, but out of shame before people and the anxious fear that he might break his rule. This toil seems righteous to bodily people and pleasing to soulish people. But to spiritual people everything done in the name of Christ is acceptable, just as our Lord Jesus Christ himself held out the hand of hope to every weakness, through the reward promised for every desire that is carried out in his name.

I will now say why this toil is great in the eyes of those who are bodily in mind, and pleasing in the eyes of those who are soulish in wisdom. Whoever is bodily in his mind knows nothing beyond what is seen in the body. Because he sees the body deprived of the things it takes its ease in, he marvels at the man who toils. And because that man has despised the desires that he himself loves, he supposes that this is the full measure of righteousness. That is why bodily toil is reckoned as righteousness in people's eyes. The Pharisees were like this. They set themselves apart from the people by their dress, by unusual footwear and by fixed fasts, and so they were reckoned righteous in the eyes of the people. But our Lord, to expose their inner selves, which did not match their outward appearance, said: 'You are the ones who justify yourselves before people, but God knows the hearts. For what is exalted among people is abominable before God' (Luke 16:15). He means: that outward form by which you appear to people

as righteous, God does not see as people do, from the outside; he looks within. And because he sees that your hearts are not pure before him, even the very thing by which you are great in people's eyes is abominable before him.

People who are soulish in wisdom take pleasure in bodily toil for this reason: their minds are trained in learning, and through the wisdom of their discernment they have come to despise outward things.

But the spiritual man glories in God with his whole mind, and so he resembles God. And because he knows each person according to his measure, his mind accepts all the differences in everyone and gives each its due praise.

These two ranks, the bodily and the soulish, are below limpidity. That is why they are accusers and fault-finders. They pass judgment on everyone's deeds, and nothing pleases them, so to speak, except the will of their own minds. The reason only the will of their own minds pleases them is that they think whatever is in their hearts is righteousness and the wisdom of all things."

Eutropius said: "You have often said that anyone whose mind is below limpidity does not understand the mystery of the other world when he hears it. We want you to explain to us why he does not understand."

The Solitary said: "Consider, my beloved, that the true birth of the true person is above limpidity. Baptism, too, which was established as a type of that new birth after the resurrection, is above purity. And that true birth of the resurrection is likewise above purity. But so that you may understand fully, consider what I am saying. Consider baptism, resurrection and limpidity, for they share one

mystery, after the likeness of the womb. The bodily birth of a person begins when he comes out of the womb in which he has been and enters the conduct of this life. In the same way, the new birth of the true person comes when he is no longer enclosed only in the purity in which he has been, but goes out from limpidity and enters the knowledge of the life of that world. The womb is made an intermediary for the unborn child, between the life of the belly and the life of this world: from the womb it comes out and enters this life. In the same way, limpidity is made an intermediary for the hidden person, between the good conduct of this life and the true life, which is the mind that has knowledge of the spiritual world: from limpidity he comes out and enters that life. A person cannot perceive or see the colours of this creation unless he has first been born from his mother's womb. In the same way, a person cannot perceive and understand the mystery of the spiritual world unless he has first been purified from all defilement, has left behind the purity of works, and stands in the life of knowledge. And because few are made worthy, through divine help, to be purified from the defilement of evils, few are those who have perceived the wisdom of the new world.

Now let me rise in my discourse to a lofty height and gather much into a few words. Above limpidity, then, is another life, that which comes after the resurrection. It is the conduct of the new person, a conduct not in works but in knowledge. In that life, good works are below purity. The whole power of the natural law and the written law reaches only as far as purity of mind. Above purity is spiritual conduct. It is called spiritual not because it has been newly perfected in the Spirit here, for this is not given apart from the new world. It is called spiritual because it moves in a knowledge higher than the soulish order that is set within the body. For in the new spirituality no one

since the world was created has lived, except our Lord Jesus Christ alone."

Eusebius said: "Then what was the rank of conduct of the righteous of old?"

The Solitary said: "They walked in the righteousness of good works, but all their uprightness extended only as far as purity of mind. For the natural law that was set within them could do nothing more than teach the mind to distinguish between good and evil. Not even God, when he lists good works in Ezekiel, calls the one who does them spiritual, but says, 'Whoever does these things is righteous' (Ezek 18:9). Nowhere does the Old Testament give anyone the name 'spiritual'. For people cannot rise above purity of mind in this life unless they receive divine revelation. How hard a person must strive to break down the fences that stand between him and purity! By fences I mean evil works, hateful passions and impure thoughts, which stand like fences before a person's mind. And how much harder it is to break through them and be beyond them, in the true vision of that world! One person breaks down the fence of fornication, and then wickedness stands as a fence before his mind. Another breaks down the fence of love of money, and envy stands as a fence before his mind, and so on with others I will not list in full. I do not think a person's nature is able to break through every one of them and come out beyond them all without God's help. But if he breaks through them all and is beyond them, he has left the conduct of this world and begun the conduct of that world, whose conduct is the true vision of its mysteries. Our Lord Jesus, however,

began to live his glorious ways above purity of mind. Not one of the passions turned him toward the vision of our world, and the vision of our world is love of it. Nor did the fence of a hateful thought ever stand before his mind, for he removed the fence that was all enmity, as Paul said: 'He removed the fence of enmity' (Eph 2:14)."

Eusebius said: "What is the fence of enmity?"

The Solitary said: "Hear it in the sense we have set ourselves to speak of. By 'fence' I mean all the hateful conduct made up of evil passions. It is called 'of enmity' because by this conduct we become enemies of God: 'You were once enemies through your evil works' (cf. Col 1:21). A fence stops the eye of the body from seeing anything beyond it. In the same way, evil conduct stops the eye of the soul from seeing the mystery of that world."

Eusebius said: "And why did the blessed Paul not say that he overthrew the fence of enmity, but that he broke through it?"

The Solitary said: "In another copy it is written that way. It is said of the enmity between the people and the nations, which was abolished through Christ. As for the rest of the sense you asked about, I will settle it for you. He did not say 'overthrew', because from long before, this hateful conduct had been firmly established throughout the whole nature of humankind, and there was no one able to break through it and be beyond it in the conduct of the new life. But when our Lord was born into our world, this fence of evil conduct could not stand before him. He broke through it by the power of his knowledge and was beyond it from the very beginning of his birth. By the breach he showed in it, he gave people the hope that they too will be beyond it after the resurrection. And by the breach he made in it, he poured light into our world from

the light of that world, which is the hope of God. Nor was the conduct of Jesus our Life-giver only above purity. It was above the two levels of knowledge that are above purity, that is, the third, that new mystery of the Spirit. For he alone overcame the world by the power of his knowledge. All the righteous were raised in their good works below purity of mind, until the coming of Christ. After his coming, God gave to certain people a wisdom that glories in the height of the Spirit. Such was the upbringing of John the Baptist in the wisdom of the mystery of Christ. The conduct of his hidden person was raised in the mystery of Christ, while his outward conduct was that of the Law, in the habit of the Nazirites. 'John came to you in the way of righteousness' (Matt 21:32). 'He ate no bread and drank no wine' (Luke 7:33).

But people who are bodily in their minds, when they see a man whose conduct is fine and who keeps himself from evils, or who stands firm in bodily toil, suppose that he is spiritual. Yet it is not only in these things that he is not spiritual. He is not spiritual at all, even if there is no filthy thought in him, which is something not to be found among human beings. For once he has been purified of these things, he is still called soulish. Because he has turned toward the good conduct of the soul, he is called soulish. The study of wisdom in a pure mind is the conduct of the soul's nature in this life, because it is the soul that carries it. The nature of the body carries wakefulness, standing and the service of toil, and it is the body that feels them. In the same way, the nature of the soul carries wisdom in a pure mind. The inner shares in the toil of the outer, because it allowed that toil to happen; and the outer shares in the inner, because it is its instrument.

For this reason they share in one reward. But if we call a man spiritual because of good works and a pure mind, what is left for him to become in that world? If he is spiritual, then by the reckoning of many he is spiritual in this life as well. But if he has not been made perfect here, it is clear that here he is soulish and will later be spiritual. You remember that I have often told you that spiritual conduct is not good works, or thoughts about good things, but the mind that shares with God in the knowledge of his mysteries. The life that people receive from God after their resurrection is higher than good works. For there we will not exist in works: in giving to the poor, clothing the naked, welcoming strangers, honouring parents, not hating or envying, people coming to good accord with one another, or being humble and merciful, and so on. In this life these things are glorious and excellent. Humility is better than haughtiness, and lowliness than pride. But there the conduct of each of us will be in a mind that springs up in the wisdom of God. And because no one has risen to the newness of spiritual knowledge, no one in the world has been made perfect as a spiritual person, except only our Lord Jesus Christ, who showed us this mystery in his own person. He alone is the new truth, which the apostle calls the body, and us the members (Eph 5:30)."

Eusebius said: "Why does he call Christ the body and the saints his members?"

The Solitary said: "Because the body possesses everything: seeing, hearing, touching, walking and the rest. That is why he calls Christ the body, to show that he is perfect in all the mysteries of truth. The believers

he calls members, to teach this. None of the members possesses the fullness of the whole body; each member has one gift: hearing for the ears, sight for the eyes, speech for the tongue, touch for the hands, walking for the feet, smell for the nostrils. In the same way, each of the saints has been given one gift from the mystery of truth. But Christ, as the body, is complete in all of them. In this sense he says to the Corinthians: 'You are the body of Christ, and members each in your place' (1 Cor 12:27). He means: even though his gifts are among you, each of you, as a member in his place, has one gift. 'For God has set in his church apostles, after them prophets, after them teachers', and so on (1 Cor 12:28). He means: all these are not found in one person; each of you has one, and all of them are found in Christ. Yet even though this interpretation is very good, it is still not spiritual but soulish. The bodily person, when Paul says 'body', thinks of a body, and a body is pictured in his mind. The soulish person understands it as I have explained, which is the sense in which the apostle also said it. But if someone could say what the truth of Christ is, he would come near to spiritual knowledge. For Paul did not say how Christ is, but that he is. And when he said that Christ is complete in all truth, he did not explain what Christ's truth is. That belongs to Christ, which he alone knows, and which will also be revealed to the saints in the new birth of that world. Not even Paul, spiritual man though he was, could have done it if he had wanted to say it. His thought would not have had the power, because in this life the nature of the motions of his soul could not break through to the newness of this mystery."

Eusebius said: "And what difference is there between soulishness and spirituality? Or is something of spirituality mixed into the nature

of the soul, so that when a person reaches it he is called spiritual, and while he remains in the nature of his soul he is called soulish?"

The Solitary said: "The difference between soulishness and spirituality is like the difference between soulishness and bodiliness. Bodiliness is not some other nature apart from the body, and spirituality is not some other nature apart from the soul. When someone turns toward the desires of the body and acts out the passions of its motions in deeds, he stands in the rank of bodiliness. When someone has turned away from the body and fulfils in good works the workings of the soul that is in it, he is called soulish, because in his works he has turned toward the soul, just as he is called bodily when he turns toward the body in his deeds. But the nature of the soul is spiritual, and the rank of its nature is not the doing of works but the knowledge of the Spirit. So if someone rises in his knowledge above the doing of good works, he is no longer in the soulish rank but in the spiritual, because he has turned toward the knowledge of the nature of his soul. The soul is spiritual, but it is called soulish because it is clothed in the body and moved by the body's senses. This, then, is how these names differ. That is why, my beloved, very few, if it must be said, have drawn near to spiritual conduct; few to soulish conduct; and the whole world to bodily conduct. The spiritual man lives in divine joy and love. The soulish man lives in his works, in fear and in loftiness of mind, unless he is humble by nature. He lives in fear of growing lax in the customs set for him. The reason the passion of boasting rules over him is this. He does not know that there is a hidden conduct, not seen in the outward members, from which he could learn how far short he falls of that hidden conduct. And so he comes to think that he is

in perfection. And because he sees people living in a bodily way, he comes to think of himself as better than they are. For this reason true humility, which comes from knowledge, is found only in the spiritual man. Our Lord, who was perfect in spiritual conduct, said: 'Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart' (Matt 11:29). I say again that the soul that has perceived its hope walks in all humility. Because of its humility and its great compassion, it is constantly sorrowful. This is not the sorrow of the world, but sorrow in the sense in which our Lord said: 'Foxes have holes and the birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head' (Luke 9:58). When the soul looks toward its hope, and looks at people, and sees where it now is, it is distressed. And again a person ponders in himself: 'Will there be joy for me after my soul is separated from the body, or will I be in distress? And what if I am left without knowledge?' This is the passion of weeping. With thoughts like these the soul cannot boast of anything. It lives constantly in the feeling of humility and sorrow, while joy lies hidden within its sorrow, and from time to time that joy is revealed in its mind. I am amazed at people who have not come near this measure of knowledge, and yet think they are humble. For the soulish man is proud both in his conduct and in his wisdom. You asked me about his conduct; I have explained not only his passion but also the cause from which he acquires it. Now hear about his wisdom, and why his knowledge makes him proud. All his wisdom comes from study and learning, and everything he knows can be put into words. He is not raised up in spiritual revelations that cannot be spoken, from whose greatness he might learn

the measure of his knowledge: that although he has perceived that these things exist, he cannot know how they are. That is why he is proud of everything he knows, since he thinks he knows the truth. Think of a man whose wealth amounts to a garment of goat's hair, who uses silver vessels and has authority over a few servants. If he thinks that what he owns is all the wealth there is, and does not see the treasures of others, his wealth leaves him with a fault, since he exalts himself over others. But if he sees the wealth of others, greater than his own, then by constantly remembering their wealth his own wealth grows small in his eyes. And if he always looks at those who have less than he does, he is constantly proud. So it is with anyone whose knowledge is slight. If he does not meet many kinds of knowledge, or see spiritual revelations within himself, the passion of pride rules over him, since he thinks he knows something. He is like those others who become interpreters of a single prophet and then grow proud of their wisdom, as though by interpreting all the prophets they had reached the limit of knowledge. They do not see, as they would if they looked with exalted knowledge, that many things were said in the scriptures which God would not have wished to be said, if people had lived righteously. But because error ruled over them through evil works, many things were said to abolish error. For example: 'You shall not worship any image or any likeness' (Exod 20:4). Or: 'By myself I have sworn, says the Lord, that every soul shall worship me' (cf. Isa 45:23). If they had been worshipping him, this would not have been said. Or: 'Turn and know that I am he' (Ps 46:11). If they had not been looking to idols, he would not have urged this on them. And there are other examples, such as 'Love the Lord your God' (Deut 6:5). If they had been living in his love, this would not

have been written. So too the many prophets who spoke of captivity, exile and the sword of the nations. If people had walked in uprightness, none of the things that were spoken and that happened in the time of the prophets would have come about. They would not have been said; something more glorious would have been said instead. As people's conduct was, so was the teaching he gave them. Many words of the prophets are spoken to abolish hateful things. For in any case, to whom did God speak: to the wise and those who do good, or to fools and those who do evil? If he spoke to fools and doers of evil, it is clear that he gave them a teaching meant to abolish their folly and their wickedness. But the mystery of the new is more powerful than the old. It is more powerful in its wealth, as much as the sea, with the wealth of its waves, is more powerful than a small lake. Shall we, then, as many people say, people who have no leisure for the wisdom of truth or for knowing great things, abandon the hope that the holy Being has graciously given us, and dwell on what was said to abolish idols? Why then do we remain in these ranks, and do not hurry to rise toward that to which Christ our teacher has directed [?] us? He is the beginning of our kingdom, and in him we are set free from servitude to foreign lordships through the hope of his unique kingdom. But people who do not love wisdom, if someone urges them to approach without fear the mystery of truth and the learning of the other world, begin to be afraid. 'Let us not investigate or search,' they say, 'in case we go astray.' Yet in the pursuit of wealth, see how they dig in the earth and dive into the sea, and do not stop to think that they might die or drown. The love of gold makes them hand themselves over to every danger. But if we had the love of truth in us, we would not cease from God, but would keep pleading

for him to reveal his hidden wisdom in us.

I will also give another cause concerning the passion of pride: how a person may avoid becoming proud in his mind through the study of wisdom. What keeps him from being proud is this: being fervent in the love of learning, not of one thing but of many. Through this love the passion of pride is held back by the fervour that seeks for the mind to learn many things.

Now you have heard the causes of these passions, and why the power of humility is lacking in the minds of bodily and soulish people. Hear how it is found in the spiritual man, in his conduct and in his knowledge. In his conduct, it comes from what I am about to say. He has perceived the hope of humankind and the glory prepared for them by the grace of God, and he marvels at God's compassion. He becomes one who honours people with love, as someone who considers how God loves human beings and how great they are in his sight. But those who have not perceived the wealth kept for human beings in the new birth come to hate people and look down on them. Think of men who are prosperous in wealth and in the honour of authority in their own city, but who go to another city and are there in a wretched appearance and poor need. All those who do not know their greatness cannot honour them with love; instead they look down on them with mockery. But if men who know the greatness of their authority see them, clearly they cannot exalt themselves over them. Instead they bear the burden of honouring them and become their friends. In just this way people hate one another in their wickedness and exalt themselves over one another in their error, because they do not perceive the exalted glory they have with the grace of God. But whoever perceives the honour that awaits them there, in all

is in humility toward people. He does not look at their lowly appearance here, but at the greatness of their glory there. Even if he sees them engaged in every kind of evil, he cannot hate them or despise them, because he knows that if people perceived what God is about to give them, they would not be angering him with their wickedness. With this thought, then, a worthy man cannot suppose of himself that he is superior to them, because he knows that they are destined to have a mind that does not even conceive of sin, and that they are being kept for the life that will spring forth in the wisdom of truth. As for the knowledge of the spiritual man, and why he is not proud in his understanding of wisdom, consider briefly what I say. His knowledge grows within the mystery that is higher than bodily and psychic things. That mystery, however, makes him perceive by revelation that it is not in the nature of his movements to grasp its truth in itself, but that the mystery is higher than anything that can be thought. That he knows it is high comes from revelation; but that he is unable to think of it as fully as it was revealed to him is the weakness of his soul, which is held in the body. Through these things, wonder at the depth of God's wisdom constantly leads him to reflect how much less this life is than the mystery to come, and that it is not in the nature of human beings to attain these things apart from the goodness of God. For this reason, in the thought of these reflections, he lives in complete humility. Consider, my beloved, these three orders which I have set out according to the measure of my mind, and the reason that brings you near to the love of God and of human beings, which I wished to make fully known to you. For if you perceive the hope that awaits you, you are freed from all the passions that cause stumbling, and you set up in your souls the image of love for human beings. And as I said above,

I say that those who have perceived the hope of human beings are possessed by a mind that is complete in good things. Suppose there were people in a village, harried by the pressure of poverty, and a king sent them an extraordinary promise that he wished them to live with him in the palace in the glory of honor. Those who perceived this promise can no longer be hostile toward these poor people; rather, even those they formerly despised they now embrace with all the love of humility. But those who did not know this mystery sent by the king not only fail to honor them, but look upon them with complete contempt. This, then, is the picture: human beings in this creation are in afflictions and troubles. But God, in his mercy and the abundance of his goodness, has made known to people the promise of great gifts in the holy Gospel. Those who have perceived the gifts of God toward human beings embrace people with perfect love. But those who have not come to understand the mystery of the hope that human beings have with the Lord of all look upon them with contempt and are filled with hatred at their deeds. For it is not right for us to look at their sins here, but at the fact that they are destined to be without sins. This is especially so with people who are baptized. Every baptized person ought to be looked upon not as in this life but as in that life, not by his deeds here but by his conduct there. Eutropius said: Since your love has said that those who have perceived the hope of human beings cannot be haters and despisers of them—look, we see that all the children of the Church hear of the gifts of the Gospel, and yet few are found who do not hate and despise their fellows. The Solitary said: Although the gift of God has been revealed to everyone, yet

not everyone has perceived it with real knowledge of it. Suppose a rich man promised little babbling children that he would give them amethyst [?] and vessels of crystal and silk. Although they heard the names, they did not know the color and appearance of the things named, so as to rejoice at the man's promises and love him. In the same way God has promised human beings the great treasures of his kingdom. Everyone hears the names, but because their understanding of the things named is weak, their thought falls short. As the apostle said: “I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18). The apostle said this as he marveled at his understanding of that greatness to come. People, however, have perceived only the name of its name; the mystery of the glory itself they do not understand. And because they know only the names of the gifts, they do not marvel at God's riches, nor have they perceived the beauty of his gifts, so that their mind might grow fervent and love him, if only for the sake of his gift. And again they despise one another, because they do not know their own hope. Therefore make it your concern to contemplate the hope to come, and you will see that you become masters of your passions. Let these things be the study of your mind, my beloved, for these are the benefits of your life. Better than the wisdom of the age, this wisdom brings you near to God. All the evils that have come upon human beings came because they were not masters of their evil passions. For what reason, then, do we think the people in the days of Noah were drowned in the waters of the flood? Because they did not know the signs of the course of the stars, or because they did not take control of their disordered movements? And for what reason did the whole settlement of the Sodomites come to an end by burning? Because they were not skilled in investigating the mystery

of astrology, or because they did not abandon the unclean lust of their heart? I have not found it written, “Blessed are those who are skilled in the craft of the revolutions of astrology,” but “Blessed are those who are blameless in the way.” All the disorder of human beings in evil things comes not from ignorance of worldly matters, but from their lack of concern about evil passions. If each person attended to understanding his passions, the whole inhabited world would be rejoicing in open peace. This is what helps a person: first of all to attend to his passions, so that after he has purified his soul from them it becomes fitting for him to seek the study of every kind of wisdom. A person whose body is afflicted with sickness and whose limbs are full of the corrosion of sores should not approach the learning of crafts; first he attends to the healing of his sores, and only after he has become healthy does the learning of any work suit him. In the same way it does not help a person to approach the study of the philosophical schools; first he must have concern for learning about his passions. And when he has become strong in the health of his soul, then the learning of everything suits him. Now one of the brothers from the East, whose name was Mar Amadia [?], had come in at that moment and had not heard what had been said on the previous days. When he heard these things, he said: “Is it things no one knows that need to be taught? Who does not know the passions of his own soul? Everyone knows what is good for him and what is bad for him.” The Solitary said: If you are so perfect, brother, in this knowledge of the passions of your soul, explain to me what I ask. Tell me about your hidden self. I am not speaking of the nature of your soul; for you will not be judged for not knowing how to show that it exists in you, and when and how, and why and what it is. Rather, I am asking for that

which God also commanded you to know. That is: since God placed in your nature the law of loving good things and hating evil things, what are the causes that have brought it about that you are not living by the good things of your nature? Why, when the nature of your soul is not bodily, does your mind love bodily things? Which passion begins in you first? Which is second, after lust? Which is the one that breeds in you fear of the world? And which are those that follow it? What is the cause that multiplies them? By what are they removed from the soul? Why are malice, envy and resentment more persistent in people than the rest of the passions? For there is someone who has been freed from love of money and yet has not been cleansed of envy. What are the thoughts that can overcome each of these passions by force? What are the movements able to abolish envy? Which are the ones that oppose malice? Which are the ones that oppose fear? Just as for each of the pains of the body remedies are known in the science of medicine, and not every one of them is healed by a mixture of one kind of roots, so for each of the passions of the soul thoughts that overcome it are known in the wisdom of the mind. I ask further: how long does each of these passions cling to the soul once one has set about abolishing it? And when a person begins to wage a contest against them, why are they not easily defeated by his victory? What is the cause that makes you divided against yourself, so that you are not at peace in your thoughts? While you hate them they dwell in you; while you rebuke them they do not move away; while you strive to abolish them they are not driven out; and even when you do not want them they remain in you. Is not your conduct in your own will? And if you are in control by your will, tell me why something dwells in you that you do not

want. And explain to me why the thought within you overcomes you—along with other questions comparable to these. Do not be deceived, my dear friend, by the opinion you have of yourself. For look: while you are sick you do not want to think that you are healthy—just as in your simplicity you supposed that you were wise. Oh, the ignorance of human beings, that things hidden in the depths of the soul seem simple to them! For what is more excellent and more powerful in truth than for a person to understand his evil passions and subject them to the rule of his will? This is why God continually praises the mind that is eager for purity of thought, with his beatitudes and through the admonitions of the scriptures. For this alone is the wisdom of truth which God placed in human nature in this life, a wisdom in which there are neither opinions nor arts. All the scriptures, and the whole of human nature through the natural law placed in it, testify that it is truth. And it is this that makes people profit in good works, as Paul, the true teacher, said. In all the other kinds of wisdom, however, arts and opinions are mixed together. And one must marvel at the error of human beings: though the knowledge of the passions of the soul is so mighty, everyone thinks he has no need to learn about the setting right of his soul. The school of Hippocrates, who were marvelous in the art of medicine, said of the knowledge of the body that “life is short and the art is long”—that is, the whole lifetime of a person, as long as he lives, is too little for his mind to grasp the learning of the rich distinctions of medicine. If, then, a person's life is too short for the wisdom concerning this body we wear, to know its composition, together with the changes of its ailments and the cause of their healing, do we dare, concerning the movements of our hidden nature, to suppose that we know the order in which its passions change, and do we think it

a contemptible knowledge for a person to understand how he may free his soul from evil passions? Truly, unless divine help is manifestly given to a person, he cannot attain purity of soul. And what is to be given us by divine operation in the new birth—that we shall be there with a pure mind—we have the naive idea that a person can reach that measure while he is in the body. I heard a man of God, who had also studied the wisdom of philosophy remarkably well, say: “I do not compare any of the kinds of wisdom with this: that a person should become wise in how to be freed from his evil passions.” And again he said: “To me, the one who drives an evil passion out of himself is greater than the one who casts a legion of demons out of a demoniac. For God does not judge the one who has demons because of them; but the one in whom evil passions dwell is held bound under God's judgment, because he has not been delivered from them. A demon, whenever it is present, has a way out, for its harm is to the body and not to the nature of the soul. But an evil passion remains in the soul after a person's death.” I myself also saw a man through whom many signs were performed, yet in his mind he was very foolish, for he was overcome by anger and curses. And though he cast demons out of others by prayer while making disciples of the pagans in the land of the Indians, he paid no attention to his own passions. This man marvelous in wisdom, of whom I spoke above, also said: “From the time I had a mind for learning, my concern has been to know what is good for me and what is bad for me, and I am still lacking in this wisdom.” See what this man says about himself! Yet foolish people suppose that by wearing the monastic habit and reading the scriptures they have attained knowledge.

But so that we do not wrong the desire of this brother of ours, I will offer him one remedy of teaching concerning his passions. These passions, brother, if a person does not fully do their will, grow weak. Lions are strong by nature, but when they are left in quiet the bitterness of their savagery comes to weakness, though it is still in them; so too, by disregarding the will of the passions, the force of their wickedness withers [?]. And just as lions grow strong in the force of their might through constant provocation and feeding, so when a person does the will of his thoughts, he incites them to grow even stronger against him. But whoever has taken the trouble to drive them out of himself, and has defeated them and expelled them from his mind—they no longer dwell in his mind as masters. Even if they pass like travelers along the road of his heart, they quickly depart when he rebukes them. Just as servants expelled from their master's house no longer have the freedom to come in as they used to, so these passions lose their freedom over the soul by remaining outside it. Then a person's mind enters into constant quiet. But what shall we say of others who, when thoughts multiply against them, instead of occupying themselves with reading so that their mind may be calmed by a good word from the turmoil of thoughts, think that by much talking or by busying themselves with affairs they can give their heart rest from the oppression of its thoughts? Do not suppose, O man, that you find comfort for the mind in the business of affairs, so that by attending to them you may overcome your thoughts. Earthly thoughts cannot abolish the thoughts of the body. Even if the distraction of affairs brings you a little relief from the evil thought that harasses your mind, do not suppose that it is defeated because you are occupied with them.

Rather, as for what is constantly stirring within you, know that you have not abolished it by gaining a victory over it. So when disordered movements stir in our mind, let us not seek the comfort of help from visible things, for there is no strength in the contemplation of visible things by which we could suppose we are able to abolish the movements of resentment from our soul. Instead let us seek it from Christ, whose thought is mighty and able to defeat all the movements that stir in the disordered will of the body. For when the blessed Paul wished to teach that by asking of Christ we can receive the power of help in our afflictions, he said: “Let us therefore draw near with open face to the throne of his grace, and receive mercy and find grace for help in the time of need” (Heb. 4:16). May God, who alone is holy, in whose holiness the worlds of glory are exalted, grant us to receive in holiness into our soul the wonder of his greatness. To him be glory for ever. Amen. Peace.
Again: The Fourth Discourse

On the following occasion, after we had prayed, we began to say to him: "Good treasures have been stored up in our souls through the conversation we had with your Excellency, and we praise and thank the One who gave you this whole gift. But we want to hear about another matter, so that we do not look vaguely on the terms used in speaking of virtue. We want to learn the force of each of them, in bodily terms and in terms of the soul. If we hear how they are distinguished, our mind will be better enlightened about the many differences that exist within virtue. When we hear of humility or of mercy, we want to know whether humility is of one order only, or whether there are differences in mercy just as there are differences in sorrow. For there is a worldly sorrow, and there is a sorrow for God's sake. There are other things as well that we need to ask about." The Solitary said: "Ask freely about whatever is in your mind, and as far as our smallness allows, we will set your mind at rest. List the terms you want to ask about." Eusebius said: "We ask about fear and sorrow; about suffering and mourning; about poverty; about mercy; about peace and tranquillity; about purity; about fasting; about

service; about sacrifices; about offering; about the altar; about the fan; about the church; about the priesthood; about love; about affection; about consolation; about joy; about the worship of God; about the race of righteousness; about standing upright; about prison; about bonds; about release; about falling; about steadfastness; about wakefulness; about sleep; about nearness to God; about communion with him; about long-suffering; about endurance; about chastity; about virginity; about vigilance; about holiness; about prayer; about silence; about sickness; about health; about kingship; about lordship; about humility; about exaltation; about laughter; about mockery; about weakness; about cutting off; about struggle; about the athlete's contest; about victory; about defeat; about armour; about battle; about trade; about treasure; about wealth; about want; about need; about courage; about profligacy; about greed; about a resting-place for the head [?]; about freedom. We beg you to tell us what the force of each of these is in the soul and in the body, distinguishing between them. For the fasting of the body is not the same as the fasting of the soul. The possessions of the body are not the same as those of the soul. The joy of the body is not the same as the joy of the spirit. The wakefulness of the body is not the same as the wakefulness of the soul. And servitude in the world is not the same as servitude to sin. But because these terms sound the same when the tongue speaks them, explain their meaning to us, so that we do not hear them vaguely in everything to which they are applied." The Solitary said: "Keep these terms in your memory, and ask about each of them in turn." Eusebius said: "I ask about the passion of fear: from

what cause does this passion arise? Is it of the body or of the soul? If it belongs to the body alone, how is the fear of God found in human beings, when it is not found in animals? And if it belongs to the soul, how can a person be afraid of obstacles, when the soul is stronger than obstacles? And since the one word 'fear' is used both for the fear of God and for the fear of the world, explain to us the different senses of this word." The Solitary said: "The fear of the world comes about because of the body. This means fear of the night, dread and anxiety over things, and fear of obstacles. The body is the cause of these, because it is the body that is subject to them. The soul, in so far as it is in the body, shares in the body's fear, even though fear is not part of its nature, because it is above harm. Fear does not arise except in a nature that is subject to every kind of harm. Someone who is subject to a person harsher than himself is the one who fears him, and he does not fear a man who is not harsher than he is. In the same way the body, being subject to everything in this world, lies under the fear of the world. But the soul, because its nature is not subject to harm, is above the fear of the world. If fear belonged to the soul, how is it that we see animals, reptiles and every other thing that lacks a soul trembling and afraid of whatever harms it? The nature of the soul is free from the seasons and from their changes; from lack of food; from the abundance of crops; from the damage of hail; from scarcity of rain; from cold air; from frosty dew; from hard snow; from freezing ice; from burning heat; from the pain of aches; from the torment of hunger; from loss of speech; from blindness of the eyes; from lameness of the feet; from crippled hands; from headache; from

[?] of the nostrils; from obstruction of the [?]; from blemishes of the body; from spots of leprosy; from damage to the [?]; from pains in the inner organs; from swelling of the spleen; from burning of the liver; from overflowing bile; from pain in the bowels; from the torment of shortness of breath; from pain in the kidneys; from bloating of the stomach; from slackness of the sinews; from heaviness of the bones; from damage to the veins; from excess of blood; from pain in the breasts; from heaviness of the head; from dropsy; from burning fever; from the many internal ailments, along with the external ones; from the frailty of old age; from loss of strength; from a bent stature; from loose limbs; from all kinds of diseases; from the torment of fire; from shivering with cold; from burns and bruises; from decay and rottenness of the body; from foul smells; from a bad reputation; from violent wars; from disturbances in one place after another; from tumult in city after city; from the gloom of darkness; from the sound of thunder; from the sight of lightning; from harm done by wild beasts; from the power of demons; from harm done by evil spirits; from terrifying dreams; from the lordship of the rulers of this world. The nature of the soul is free from all these things, while the nature of the body is subject to them all, and apart from them there is no fear of the world. Why have I listed all these things? Only to show how empty love of the body is. People love this thing that is subject to all these, which has all these set over it as masters. Yet when the time comes for them to be released from the body, and by that release to be freed from all these harms, they grieve, they are distressed, they groan. And no one turns with love and joy to the soul, which is released from all these obstacles. Just as they are grieved that the body is subject to all these things, so they ought to rejoice

in their hidden man, who is above them all. Nor is the nature of the soul free from these things only: it does not even need the help that creation provides. It is not helped by the rising of the light, nor by the rest of sleep, nor by the possession of wealth, nor by the power of rank, nor by the comfort of food, nor by sweet scents, nor by songs of entertainment. How could we place a nature that is not under the authority of the world under the fear of the world? But when the soul does not look toward the body, though it is placed in the body, and turns toward what is its own, its fear is this: fear that comes from error, dread that comes from ignorance. When it turns toward the body, and soul and body are blended in a single mind, then this is the fear a person has toward the world: dread and fear of the harms I have listed. The fear directed toward God, when soul and body are of one mind together, is this: fear of judgment, dread of condemnation, terror of the torment of Gehenna, fear of the wrath of God. But when the soul knows that it is stronger than the body, its fear is this: that it may not be found worthy of the greatness to come; that it may be robbed of that true wisdom; that it may become a stranger to the mysteries of God. This is how the passion named by the word 'fear' is distinguished." Eusebius said: "You have spoken richly and gloriously, and I do not think anyone could have spoken about this life more profitably or more wisely than you have." The Solitary said: "Write down the terms you listed and give them to me, and I will speak about them one at a time as far as I am able." Eusebius said: "We have heard how fear is distinguished.

Now take those terms and tell us about them. On sorrow." The Solitary said: "Bodily sorrow is sorrow over visible things. Sorrow over provoking God by sins is a good mind, and the knowledge of the soul has a share in it. Then there is sorrow that is not mixed with the mind of the flesh, but springs from the movements of knowledge. This happens when someone perceives the greatness to come, considers what creation is, examines the glorious nature of the soul, and grieves over the body in which it is held a weak prisoner. On the passion of mourning. When the passion of mourning is over worldly things, it is bodily. When it is over debts and follies, it is the mind turning toward its hope. When it is over the humbling of the hidden man, it is the excellence of knowledge. On poverty. Poverty of the body is being stripped of possessions, and also lacking healthy senses. Poverty in possessions lies outside a person; poverty in the soundness of the limbs lies in his nature. Poverty of the soul toward the world is being stripped of hateful thoughts, and being stripped of hateful thoughts is the wealth of its knowledge. But the poverty of its nature in this life is lack of knowledge, deficient understanding and little discernment. On being stripped. Bodily stripping is the abandonment of possessions. The soul's stripping is putting off the passions. Spiritual stripping is the end of opinions. Here we strip ourselves of possessions, and we can also strip ourselves of the passions; but being stripped of opinions belongs to the life after the resurrection. On mercy. Bodily mercy means giving

alms, helping the sick, feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, bringing relief to the oppressed, and so on. The soul's mercy means having pity on those who wrong us, forgiving our enemies, showing compassion to those who injure us, and doing good to our persecutors. Spiritual mercy means having pity on those who stray, teaching those who lack understanding, and bringing near: the idle to the true prize, those far away to nearness with God, strangers to intimacy with his mysteries, the lost to being found; and to those without hope it means proclaiming hope. This is spiritual mercy, which is fulfilled in deed toward the hidden man. And this is the showing forth of God's mercy toward the human race. On peace. Bodily peace is offering a word of reconciliation to someone who is angry with us. The soul's peace, which is perfect in the soul, is being reconciled from the heart in the simplicity of peace, without deceitful words and without hidden anger. On tranquillity. Bodily tranquillity means the end of wars, quiet in the regions, submission without rebellion, no struggle for leadership, no plundering of possessions, no strife or quarrelling, no accusations in court, freedom from slander, no disputes about the faith, a harmony of quiet free from struggle. The soul's tranquillity is a heart not troubled by thoughts, a mind not divided over its reflections, a will not at war with itself, a calm thought that does not disturb the heart, the rest of the soul without confusion in its movements. Spiritual tranquillity is a mind not divided about the truth, a soul not confused by opinions, the harmony of the worlds, the peace that is in truth, their movements in truth. This tranquillity belongs to the life after the resurrection. On purity. Purity of the body means washing off filth, cleanness

of the limbs, clean clothes, a pleasant smell. Purity of the soul is being purified from the defilement of the body, being cleansed from the uncleanness of filthy thoughts, clean reflections, bright thoughts, sound movements. Spiritual purity is being raised above the world, no longer remembering its affairs, thought that dwells in God, gazing on him continually. Purity of this kind belongs to the life after the resurrection. On fasting. Bodily fasting means going hungry for food, abstaining from meals, refraining from rich fare. The soul's fasting means hungering and thirsting for righteousness, and fasting from evil conduct. Spiritual fasting means fasting from the memory of evil deeds, from thinking about them, and from recalling hateful things. This order, in which hateful things no longer rise up in our memory, belongs to the life after the resurrection. On service. Service of the body means fulfilling its desires, seeking possessions, loving mammon. Service of the soul means seeking life, loving teaching, finding wisdom, turning away from the body, caring for the soul. Bodily service toward God is vows and offerings, according to the custom of the law of Israel, which was bound to bodily service. The soul's service toward God is singing with feeling, and pure thoughts in a clean mind. Spiritual service toward God is wonder at God, the praise that arises from the depth of the mind at the greatness of his wisdom. This is beyond the power of this life, and is kept for us in the life after the resurrection. On sacrifices and offerings. A bodily offering is when a person offers to God things that lie outside himself. The soul's offering is when a person offers himself

to God by sacrificing his body. A spiritual offering is the mystery of communion with God, when a person at all times offers in his prayer pure thoughts, lifted up in their movements by wonder at God. On the altar. The bodily altar is the one modelled on the table of the people, on which the dead bodies of animals used to be laid. The hidden altar of the soul is the mind raised above itself, pleasing God by good works in remembrance of the sacrifice of Christ. The spiritual altar is the mind that is raised above the memory of the world and stirs up in its knowledge wonder at God. On the fan. A bodily fan is something the hand holds to fan with, as when Abraham drove off the birds so they would not settle on the divided pieces. The fan of the soul is the mind that holds good reflection, with which it drives filthy thoughts out of the mind. The spiritual fan is the mind that flutters with wondrous movements concerning God. On the church. The visible church in our world is a multitude of people, the gathering of the people, their association with one another. The true church is harmony of mind, peace of thought in a single faith. As for the church in heaven (Hebrews 12:23), meaning the heavenly assemblies: they are not called a church because they dwell in places and come together with one another. Rather, their church of truth is the knowledge of truth, in which they delight in the divine mysteries. On priestly service. Priestly service is bodily when someone serves as priest in a particular place and spot over bodily things, according to the law of the priests of Israel. The priesthood fulfilled in the soul is when the mind offers pure thoughts to God in pure prayer.

On love and affection. Bodily love between people is the body's attachment to everything that belongs to the body. The soul's love between people is the discipline of teaching and the study of wisdom. Spiritual love between people is divine love, the greatness of their glory, the knowledge of their hope. When someone loves God for the sake of visible things, his love is bodily. Whoever loves him for the sake of the promises, his love is of the soul. When someone loves God for himself alone, with no outside cause, this is spiritual love. This love is kept for us in the life after the resurrection. On consolation and joy. Bodily consolation and joy are wealth, health, prosperity [?], beauty and the like. The soul's consolation is the converse of good speech, the reading of the Scriptures, the finding of wisdom. Spiritual consolation is the expectation of the resurrection, hope in God, the knowledge of the world to come. This joy is not found fully in this life, but is kept for us for the life after the resurrection. On worship. Bodily worship is kneeling, bowing the back, lying prostrate on the ground. In appearance this worship is the same whether it is offered to God or to human beings. But since it is not fitting that we worship God in the same way as we bow down to people, the teaching of the Gospel requires of us a worship more excellent than the bodily: 'Those who worship God must worship him in spirit and in truth' (John 4:24). Worship in spirit, in our way of life, is a contrite mind in earnest supplication, a heart that groans with sighs. Now, in a different manner, about the remaining terms. So that we need not give these three distinctions for each of these terms, what

we have said distinctly about the body, the soul and the spiritual is sufficient. As for the rest that remain, hear them as they apply to the excellent conduct of the soul. The excellent race, my beloved, is the seeking of wisdom. The excellent prison is a mind that does not wander among evils. The lowly bonds are the senses that do not run in the way of wisdom. Release that brings relief is a mind not bound by desires. Sinking down from the height of knowledge is the fall of the soul. The soul's standing upright is when it stands in the authority of its freedom. Wakefulness of mind is good meditation. The soul's sleep is the ceasing of good thought. Nearness to God is obedience to the commandments. Communion with God is clinging to his love. Long-suffering in afflictions is the soothing of pains. Enduring in teaching is laying up profitable trade. Chastity of mind is modesty of thought. True virginity is a soul that has not been joined in love of the body. Vigilance of heart is not leaning toward the world. Bodily humility is a well-ordered appearance with a calm reply in speech. Humility belongs to the soul when it places itself in lowliness beneath everyone. Asking for invisible things is spiritual prayer. Bodily silence is the ceasing of speech. The soul's silence is a mind not at strife in its thoughts. Spiritual silence is when the soul does not think up opinions. True lordship is the subduing of evil movements. Exaltation of the body is boasting in possessions. Exaltation of the soul is boasting in knowledge. The soul's laughter is mockery. The excellent struggle is the battle against the passions. The true contest is victory over evil thoughts. The victory of the soul is the true kingship. The armour of the mind is the clothing of wisdom. Helpful trade is

teaching about good things. Lasting wealth is a hidden treasury of the soul. Courage worthy of praise is when someone overcomes his own evil will. Even demons are able to carry off the riches of the world; their strength is enough to tear down walls and kill people; but they have no wish to conquer the hostility of their own envy. The strength of the soul, my beloved, is this: when it hears the opinions of heresies, it is not scandalized and does not hate those who hold them. If it hates, that is weakness of soul; and just as the body is overcome by a blow, the soul is struck down by stumbling. Profligacy and greed, when mixed with the mind of the flesh, mean never having enough of the evils of others. The natural greed of the soul is never having enough of the study of wisdom. Thirst for spiritual mysteries is the pleasure of the new life. Bodily pleasure means never being filled with the choicest foods of the world; in the same way, never having enough of the wisdom of that world is a spiritual pleasure that refreshes and gladdens the inner man. Bodily freedom means being free of insolence and falsehood, speaking truthfully, and being faithful in what has been entrusted to us. The soul's freedom is release from the body, not being enslaved to the mind of the flesh. Yet, my beloved, this is not yet the freedom of the life after the resurrection, since in its seeking the soul is still enslaved to wandering passions. A soul that has not been released from everything, though it bears the image of God in its mind, is not yet equal to the freedom of Christ, who is neither bound by love of visible things nor wanders in thought as he seeks. For if the soul has been released from the passions of the body, but has fallen back in another way into passions and wandering thoughts, it has placed a yoke of servitude on itself. Though released from the will of the body, it is once more enslaved to creation in its seeking.

And because of this seeking it also lives in fear that it may fall into error. Unless the seeking that wanders comes to an end, fear does not end. But in spiritual freedom there is no enslavement to the memory of the world, no recollection of creation, no wandering among the elements, no inquiry into how they are composed, no love of knowing them, no love of earthly wisdom, and no opinions about that wisdom. That freedom is not enslaved to error. It is the true freedom of Christ, which is the kingdom of the worlds, the freedom the worlds are destined to receive. Let us too, my beloved, ask and plead that God in his mercy and goodness may make us worthy of it, in that harmony of the worlds of glory. Therefore, my beloved, let us draw near to the glorious order of the conduct of the inner man. Let us keep away from attachment to the hateful things that God hates. Let us not let our mind settle in regions of thought that have no rest from the struggle of battle. Let us settle our soul in the calm place where nothing hinders its tranquillity. Let us not abandon our mind to thoughts that are thought outside the will of God. Let us bind our knowledge to the thought of the knowledge of the Lord of all. Let there be no sluggishness in us to hold our life back from the labour of good works. Let us beware of the hidden sleep that has no sight of the truth. Let us not leave the filth of sin in our soul, or spiritual beauty will loathe it. Let us scour the thought of our heart clean of the rust of the world's thinking. Let us not bring low the movements of our soul by enslaving them to the comfort of the body. Let us please God by keeping his will steadfast in us. Let us not become estranged from love of his laws through love of the works of sin. Let us gain the confidence of an unveiled face before him through afflictions endured for his name's sake. Let us not place ourselves under the mark of his rebuke by scorning to keep his law. Let us lift our life above condemnation

by keeping the commandments of the just Lord. Let us not lose our adoption as sons by becoming estranged from God. Let us be eager to become heirs of the Father's promises by scorning the things that pass away. Let the thought of our heart not be fixed on visible things. Let us always love to meditate on the things that are not set before the sight of the eyes. Let us not be bound by things from which we must be released. Instead, let us seek bonds that hold our senses fast in the love of God, so that when we are released from the body, which is full of passions, we may be found in the place of the joys that are in God, to whom be glory for ever. Amen. Here ends the book of John the Solitary.
